en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huiyuan.
In the sixteenth [section], the first part, "The Deva Vidyut said," marks the individual discourse. Below, it reveals what was taught.

"The two—clarity and ignorance"—reversely cites these two characteristics. There are two types of analysis: first, the explanation according to their characteristics. [This refers to] darkness and delusion.
When the mind conditions an object but does not comprehend it, this is called ignorance (*avidyā*); when wisdom conditions an object and clearly comprehends it, this is called clarity (*vidyā*).
Second, explained with reference to the mind:
the nature of the deluded mind is darkness; even if there is conditional understanding, it is still ignorance.
Just as a person in a dream possesses discrimination while its nature is one of昏睡 (torpid sleep), so too is the nature of pleasant sensation one of 行苦 (the suffering of conditioned existence).
The nature of the true mind is illuminating and is therefore called clarity; even the inherently pure mind during the stage of an ordinary being is likewise called clarity.
Now, following the latter approach,
these two are translated below to clarify non-duality.
Within this approach, truth and delusion are of the same essence, thereby constituting non-duality.
First there is the analysis, followed by the conclusion.
To say that "ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself clarity" means that when delusion is realized, it is itself the truth.
The substance of the deluded mind is in fact the true mind; therefore, the nature of ignorance is itself clarity, just as the substance of deep sleep is itself the retributive mind.
This sentence concludes the correct elucidation of the meaning of "not three.
As for the statement, "Even illumination cannot be grasped," this distinguishes the true from the false.
Why is such a distinction necessary?
When people hear of this illumination, they attempt to grasp it as something to be treated through its corresponding conditions.
To prevent this view, it is said that this illumination cannot be grasped as something to be treated through its corresponding conditions.
"Illumination is called ungraspable" means it is free from all numerical categories; this explains the preceding point that it cannot be grasped by treating it through its conditions.
This "clarity" belongs to the side of the deluded mind and is subsumed under the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*).

As for what is called "clarity," it is the essence of the true mind; the equality-nature of the true mind is like space, transcending all numerical categories. Therefore, it cannot be grasped as being identical to the object-condition or its antidote.
It may also be said that within this, the two characteristics are simultaneously discarded to constitute non-duality.
To say that "the nature of ignorance is itself clarity" discards the characteristic of ignorance;
since the true nature of ignorance is clarity, it cannot be grasped unilaterally.
Detached from all numerical categories, one eliminates their manifest characteristics.
When both characteristics are extinguished, it is called "non-duality.
This is the understanding of non-duality.
The phrase "in which there is neither equality nor duality" explains the meaning of their entry [into the Dharma].
The section beginning with "This is... concludes [the preceding discussion].
In the seventeenth [section], the initial words "Sukhadarśana said" introduce the individual who speaks separately.
The following clarifies what has been taught, first through analysis and subsequently by way of conclusion.
Within the middle section, the discussion first concerns the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and later the remaining aggregates.
Regarding the aggregate of form, the phrase "the two aspects of form and emptiness" is stated as a counter-illustration of these two characteristics.
Next, there are three explanations:
first, that matter is called "empty" because it is not the self; this is as explained in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Second, that within the conventionally designated matter there is no fixed nature, which is called "empty"; this is as explained in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Third, the conventional designation of the characteristics of form is also non-existent; this is termed "emptiness," and it exists only in the Great [Vehicle].
The meaning discussed here consistently follows the third [position].
Turning these two [truths] downward reveals non-duality.
Within this gate, the two truths sharing the same essence is termed "non-duality"; it does not involve the total negation or elimination [of phenomena].
"Form is itself emptiness" clarifies that existence is itself non-existence.
The appearance of clouds constitutes form, yet form is itself formlessness; therefore, form is emptiness.
The phrase "emptiness does not arise from the extinction of form" distinguishes this from the emptiness resulting from the cessation of phenomena through the application of antidotes.

The phrase "the nature of form is itself empty" distinguishes this from the emptiness that results from analyzing causes and effects; it is like the water in a mirage, whose intrinsic nature is not water, and which does not depend on the analysis of its constituent particles and elements to be found as non-existent water.
Form is also like this: its self-nature is empty and non-existent; it does not depend on the division of objects and the great elements to be empty, which is called "emptiness of self-nature.
The same applies to the remaining aggregates (*skandhas*) below; there too, two [extremes] are negated, and subsequently non-duality is clarified, with the phrasing identical to what precedes.
This interpretation is non-dual.
The phrase "to penetrate therein" explains the meaning of "entry.
The section beginning with "this is" serves as the conclusion.
In the eighteenth [section], the initial phrase “The mark of dawn said” indicates a specific person’s distinct explanation.
What follows clarifies that which was spoken.
Regarding the statement “the four kinds are different from the element of space,” two characteristics are cited in contrast.
The statement regarding "four kinds of difference" clarifies that there is a space distinct [from the elements].
Earth, water, fire, and wind constitute the four kinds; this separate space is termed "difference.
Alternatively, the four great elements may each be individually termed "difference."
Regarding "the emptiness-element is different": this clarifies that emptiness is distinct from existence; because emptiness and existence are mutually different, they are called "two.
Below, these two are reversed to clarify "non-duality.
Within this gate, the fact that these two dharmas share the same essence is termed "non-duality."
First there is the analysis, followed by the conclusion.
To state that "the four great elements are themselves emptiness" is the correct understanding of non-duality.
Because the four great elements lack intrinsic nature and lack characteristics, they are therefore emptiness.
The statement, "Just as the prior limit and the posterior limit are empty, so too is the middle limit empty," serves as an analogy to reveal non-duality.
Birth-and-death is the prior limit, nirvana is the posterior limit, and the noble path is called the middle; because the prior and posterior limits are empty, the middle limit is also empty.
The same applies to the four great elements.
This explanation is non-dual.
"If one can thus know all lineages" explains the meaning of "entry.
"This is" and below is the conclusion.
In the nineteenth section, the initial phrase "Wondrous Intention said" marks the person who speaks and distinguishes their discourse.
What follows clarifies the content of the teaching, first through analysis and subsequently by conclusion.
Within the analysis, non-duality is elucidated by means of the twelve bases (*āyatana*); first, it is discussed with reference to the eye and form.
"Eye and form constitute duality" reversely cites these two characteristics.
Below, these two are overturned to clarify non-duality; by simultaneously discarding both characteristics, one arrives at non-duality.

"If one knows that the nature of the eye is neither greed for, nor aversion toward, nor delusion regarding forms, this is called 'quiescence'"; this refutes and dispels the characteristics of the eye.
Emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of this eye; within this nature of the eye, there is no expectation.
Since the eye does not exist, who could give rise to greed, hatred, or delusion toward forms?
Because greed and the others do not arise, it is called "quiescence.
This specifically refutes the eye and refutes form; other matters are not discussed.
If it were set forth in full detail, one should also say: "If one knows the nature of form, such that the eye is without greed, without hatred, and without delusion, this is called tranquility.
For now, only one side has been cited; the other side may be understood accordingly.
In the remaining entries below, the same method is employed: first the duality is raised, and subsequently non-duality is clarified.
This clarification of non-duality is explained specifically with respect to the underlying intention; the other cases may be understood by analogy.
The phrase "abiding therein" serves as a summary that reiterates the point for the sake of entering into non-duality.
In the twentieth [section], "Akṣayamati said" marks the specific speaker for his distinct discourse.
Below, that which is spoken is revealed, first through analysis and subsequently by way of conclusion.
Within the analysis, the meaning of non-duality is first explained, followed by the explanation of the meaning of "entering."

Regarding the resolution of non-duality within the absence of duality, the non-duality is distinguished by means of the six perfections and the mind of dedication; first, it is explained with reference to giving and dedication.
The phrase "the duality of giving and dedication to omniscience" reversely cites these two characteristics.
The fruit and virtue of all Buddhas is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*); to employ one's own practice and dedication in order to seek that virtue is termed "dedication toward all-knowledge.
Below, these two are reversed to constitute "non-duality."
Within this gate, the two characteristics being of one and the same essence is called "non-duality," not that they are to be destroyed or eliminated.
Regarding the statement, "The nature of giving is itself the nature of the wisdom of dedication," there are two interpretations:
first, speaking in terms of emptiness, they share the same single emptiness-nature; [the second is as follows].
Secondly, according to the teaching on existence, these two both take the true mind as their nature; because their essence is not distinct, they are said to be "non-dual.
In the subsequent perfections (pāramitās), the same sequence is followed—first presenting the two and subsequently clarifying their non-duality—the text being explained in the same manner as before.
This interpretation is non-dual.
The phrase "entering into the single characteristic therein" explains the meaning of "entering.
The section beginning with "This is" serves as the conclusion.
In the twenty-first section, the initial phrase “Deep Wisdom said” marks the person who speaks individually.
What follows clarifies that which is spoken.
The passage “This emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness” (2) reverses [the previous] by citing two characteristics.
These three are explained in detail as in the chapter on the three liberations.
Although there are these three types, why are they called "two"?
They are called two because they are distinct.
Furthermore, within this context, the mutual opposition of two things is also termed "two.
Herein, these two are reconciled as non-dual.
Within this gate, the identity of the two phenomena constitutes non-duality.
"Emptiness is signlessness, and signlessness is wishlessness"—this dispels their distinct characteristics.
Within the single principle of emptiness, three aspects are distinguished according to their respective meanings; thus, they attain mutual identity.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said: "In the Mahāyāna, the three gates of liberation are one in essence.
If a person enters emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they simultaneously know signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*);
likewise, even when entering wishlessness, they also know emptiness and signlessness."
Regarding the statement, "If there is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, then there is no mind, thought, or consciousness," this serves to dispel particularized conceptions.
Because one grasps through particularized and distorted conceptions, it is necessary to dispel them.
The terms *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* are explained as being synonymous in general; however, they are distinguished within this context:
the seven consciousnesses are called *citta* because they are the basis for the accumulation [of seeds];
the six consciousnesses are called *manas* because they are said to be similar in their engagement with objects (*viṣaya*).
The five consciousnesses are called "consciousness" because they cognize present objects.
These three distinctions are as explained in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
When investigated according to principle, the substance of these three is empty, their characteristics do not exist, and their functions cannot be apprehended; therefore, they are all non-existent.
The preceding section refuted the distinct [liberations] in order to return to their unity.
Now, regarding the statement "in one liberation there are precisely three liberations," by contemplating the one as opening into the many, it establishes the meaning of the previous point.
The following summarizes this: one who knows in this way is said to have "entered non-duality.
The phrase "This is" concludes [the section].
Among the twenty-two [statements], the first—"Śāntendriya said"—identifies the person and introduces their individual discourse.
The following clarifies what was taught:
"The two of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha" refers back to the two characteristics.
Since the characteristics of the Three Jewels are twofold, they are called "two."
Furthermore, among these three, two are said to be relative and are thus also called "two.
The meaning of the Three Jewels is as extensive as discussed in a separate chapter; this should be fully expounded there.
Below, these two are reconciled to form non-duality.
Within this gateway, different phenomena sharing the same essence are termed "non-dual" (*advaya*); this does not imply a negation through refutation.
First, there is the analysis, followed by the conclusion.
Within the analysis, the meaning of non-duality is first explained.
"The Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Sangha. By demonstrating the mutual identity of these distinct aspects, non-duality is revealed.
This refers to the "Three Jewels of One Substance" within the sutras, also known as the "homogeneous substance" (samāna-kāya).
What is the meaning of this?
Generally, there are four ways of explaining it:
first, distinguishing oneness based on phenomena.

Within the single fruit of Buddhahood, three aspects are distinguished according to their respective meanings: the meaning of awakening is called "Buddha"; that which serves as a standard for emulation is called "Dharma"; and the exhaustion of all impurities and transgressions is called "Saṃgha.
This single principle applies universally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; even the *Abhidharma* contains this same meaning.
Second, regarding the refutation of the principle of substantial nature, we distinguish one point:
although the Three Jewels differ, they all lack a fixed nature; because this principle of the absence of nature is uniform, they are said to be "of the same essence" (*samavāya*).
This applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; even the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* contains this meaning, so it is not found in the Mahāyāna alone.
Third, regarding the principle of the emptiness of the destruction of characteristics, there is one point to be distinguished:
although the Three Jewels are distinct, they are all empty and without characteristics; not only do they lack intrinsic nature, but their characteristics themselves do not exist.
The principle of signlessness is one; therefore, they are said to be of the same substance.
This applies exclusively to the Great [Vehicle].
Fourth, within the gateway of true dependent origination, their oneness is distinguished.

The Three Jewels all take the *tathāgatagarbha*—the Buddha-nature—as their essence; for it is through the principle of the mind of true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) arising and assembling as dependent origination that the Three Jewels are established. Within this framework, one [aspect] is taught as indeterminate.
If one distinguishes the Three Jewels by reference to *nirvāṇa*, all three take *nirvāṇa* as their essence; therefore, they are said to be of one essence.
Thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, a bodhisattva reflects: "In what way are these three things of one essence with me?"
The Buddha himself explained:
"I say that these three things are Great Nirvāṇa; therefore, they are called a single essence (*eka-rasa*).

If one distinguishes the Three Jewels by means of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), all three take Buddha-nature as their essence; therefore, they are called a single essence. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "These three refuges are precisely my own nature."

If one distinguishes the Three Jewels according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the Three Jewels all take ultimate truth as their essence; thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one can contemplate that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding and identical to ultimate truth."

If one discusses the Three Jewels from the perspective of the meaning of permanence, the Three Jewels all take permanence as their essence and are thus termed "one essence. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "I do not say that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha lack the characteristic of non-differentiation; I only say that they are non-differentiated in being permanent, eternal, and immutable."
If one distinguishes the Three Jewels from the perspective of the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), all three take the principle of emptiness as their essence.
If one discerns the Three Jewels from the perspective of the gate of non-duality (*advaya*), they are equally taken to have non-duality as their essence; such is the case for everything.
This "all as one" is not a mere numerical oneness.
What is discussed here is explained according to the gateway of true dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
When the single True Suchness (*tathatā*) arises as three through dependent origination, all three are suchness: the Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Sangha.
The preceding discussion of the identity of individual characteristics states that "these Three Jewels are all unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) to collectively manifest their non-duality.
Since the Three Jewels are entirely the True Suchness (*tathatā*), the eternal Dharma, they are all unconditioned.
"Equal to space" is illustrated by analogy:
just as dust and space are unimpeded and immovable, they are distinguished according to their respective meanings, yet their essence is one.
The Three Jewels are thus; therefore, their essence is one.

As for the statement, "All dharmas are likewise," it means that because these Three Jewels are of a single essence and non-dual, all dharmas are likewise of a single essence; hence it is said, "likewise."
This explanation is non-dual.
"Able to conform to this practice" explains the meaning of "entering.
The phrase "this is called" concludes [the section].
Among the twenty-three [sections], "The Unobstructed One says" marks the person who speaks and distinguishes him from others.
What follows clarifies that which is spoken.
"The two regarding the body and the cessation of the body" reversely cites these two characteristics.
Birth and death are termed "body," and the extinction of the body into nirvana is termed "extinction of the body. Existence and non-existence are two distinct parts, which are termed "duality.
Here, these two are overturned to clarify non-duality; by simultaneously discarding both aspects of duality, one arrives at non-duality.
First the analysis, then the conclusion.
Within the analysis, the statement "the body is itself the cessation of the body" briefly clarifies non-duality.
Since the absence of location of the body and the absence of location of that body’s cessation share the same principle, it is said that they are "identical."
The following section provides an explanation, first posing a question and then offering a resolution.

Regarding the phrase, "Seeing the precious marks of the body, one does not give rise to views of the body or views of its extinction," this means that by contemplating the unity [of the body], one breaks through [the notion of] individuality.
The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is the true mark of the body; within this reality, there has never been a body from the outset, so what is there to be extinguished?
Therefore, seeing the true nature of the body, one does not give rise to the view of a body nor the view of its extinction.
"Body and the extinction of the body are neither two nor different": this refutes difference to establish unity.
Since both body and its extinction are equally non-existent, they are said to be "not two"; this eliminates the characteristic of difference.
Since these two characteristics no longer exist, the grasping mind also ceases; this is called "non-discrimination," which dispels the notion of distinct entities.
The preceding analysis is now complete.
The statement, "To be neither startled nor afraid within this is to enter non-duality," reiterates the point to conclude it.

Sentient beings of the Hīnayāna, upon hearing it said that there is no body and that even cessation is non-existent, generally give rise to fear; therefore, [the Buddha] suddenly proclaims this so that they may not be startled or terrified, neither feeling astonishment at the non-existence of cessation nor fear at the non-existence of the body.
Furthermore, there is nowhere in the body that does not cause alarm, and nowhere in the cessation of that body that does not cause fear.
When understood through their commonality, the meaning is identical.
The phrase "This is" below serves as the conclusion.
Among the twenty-four [sections], the first, "The Superior Good Says," marks the individual who speaks.
The subsequent part clarifies what is said.
"Goodness of body, speech, and mind" reverses the order to cite two characteristics.
They are called "two" because they are distinct.
Furthermore, within them, each pair of opposites is also termed "two.
By reversing these two below, one clarifies "non-duality"; the simultaneous negation of both dualistic characteristics constitutes non-duality.
First there is the analysis, followed by the conclusion.
Within the analysis, the meaning of "non-duality" is first explained.
The statement, "These three karmas are all without action," generally clarifies non-duality.
When one investigates them to their ultimate limit, they are all empty; since no dharma can arise, they are called "all non-action.
"The mark of non-action of the body is itself the non-action of speech; the mark of non-action of speech is itself the non-action of mind"—this specifically reveals non-duality.
Since there is no distinction between non-existence and meaninglessness, they are mutually identical.
Regarding the statement, "These three non-creations are the non-creative characteristic of all phenomena," this reiterates the preceding category to clarify that all phenomena are entirely non-dual.
The phrase "One who can thus follow non-conceptual wisdom" explains the meaning of "entering.
The section beginning with "This is" serves as the conclusion.
Among the twenty-five [categories], the first, "The Field of Merit," identifies the person previously discussed.
The following clarifies what was taught:
"Meritorious action, demeritorious action, and immovable action—these two" refers to the presentation of two characteristics by way of contrast.

Actions that constitute the evil karma of the three miserable realms (*durgati*) and the karma for specific retributions of suffering among humans and devas are called demeritorious action. All wholesome karma of humans and devas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as the karma for specific retributions of pleasure among hungry ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*), is called meritorious action. The karma of meditative stillness in the two higher realms is termed immovable action.
The following section reverses these two to clarify non-duality; by simultaneously discarding both dualistic marks, one arrives at non-duality.
This consists of an initial analysis followed by a conclusion.
In the analysis, the first statement—“the true nature of the three practices is itself emptiness”—dissolves the distinction to return to unity.
Emptiness is without sin, merit, or movement, for it dispels distinctions through oneness;
this is the explanation of non-duality.
"Not giving rise to these three activities" explains the meaning of that person.
The phrase "This is" below serves as the conclusion.
Among the twenty-six [sections], the first—"The Flower Adornment says"—identifies the person who speaks individually.
The following portion reveals what was taught.
"Arising from me as two" refers back to the two characteristics.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the conventional person (*pudgala*) who is their composite are designated as "me" (*ātman*); all phenomena (*dharma*) produced by that [person] are designated as "arisen from me" (*mamotpanna*). These are the two distinct names.
The following section reverses these two to clarify non-duality; the simultaneous elimination of the two characteristics constitutes non-duality.
First there is the analysis, followed by the conclusion.
Regarding the phrase "seeing my true nature does not give rise to duality," this refers to the refutation and elimination of the two characteristics.
The principle of non-self is the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the self; within this true mark, there is fundamentally no self, so how could anything arise?
Therefore, one does not give rise to duality.
"Not abiding in dual dharmas, there is no consciousness" means to eliminate and dispel dualistic attachments.
"Non-perception is the entry into non-duality": this restates the preceding to conclude it.
Among the twenty-seven [sections], the first, "Virtue-Treasury said," identifies the person and provides a specific explanation.
The following clarifies what is being explained.
"The two [aspects] of 'that which is attained'" refers back to these two characteristics.

The performance of good and evil resulting in the attainment of suffering and pleasure is termed "that which is attained"; within this "that which is attained," the distinctions such as suffering and pleasure are designated as "the two."
The following section reverses these two [concepts] to clarify non-duality; by simultaneously discarding both aspects of duality, one arrives at non-duality.
First there is the analysis, followed by the conclusion.

"If there is nothing to be attained and nothing to be grasped or rejected" means that within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), what is attained is fundamentally non-existent; because there is nothing to be attained, there is no pleasure to be grasped and no suffering to be rejected.
"One who neither grasps nor rejects" is the summary statement that concludes the section.
Within the twenty-eight [sections], the first, "Candrottarā said," identifies the person and introduces their specific discourse;
the following clarifies what was spoken.
"Darkness and light are two" reverses [the previous statement] to cite two characteristics.
Afflictions, which are dark delusions, are called "darkness," while wisdom is called "light.
Below, these two are overturned to clarify non-duality; by simultaneously discarding both characteristics, one realizes non-duality.
First the analysis, then the conclusion.
Within the analysis, the meaning of non-duality is clarified first.
"Without darkness and without light, there are no two"—this briefly analyzes it.
The section beginning with "Therefore" provides an explanation, first posing a question and then offering a resolution.
"Just as entering the meditative absorption of cessation is without darkness and without light" is a profound metaphorical illustration.
"The characteristics of all dharmas are likewise so" applies the metaphor to reveal the Dharma.
This interpretation is non-dual.
The phrase "entering into equality therein" explains the meaning of "entry.
The section beginning with "This is" serves as the conclusion.
Within the twenty-ninth [section], "The Jewel-Seal Hand said," introduces the speaker for a specific exposition.
Below, that which is expounded is revealed.
"Delighting in nirvāṇa and not delighting in the world" (verse 2) presents two characteristics by way of contrast.
The following section reverses these two to clarify non-duality; by simultaneously dispelling both dualistic marks, one arrives at non-duality.
This consists of an initial analysis followed by a conclusion.
Within the analysis, the initial statement—“To neither delight in nirvana nor loathe the world is to have no duality”—briefly clarifies its characteristics.
The section beginning with "Therefore" provides an explanation, first posing a challenge and then offering a resolution.
To say, "If there were bondage, then there would be liberation," is an explanation by way of negation (*pratiṣedha*) to demonstrate non-duality.
To say, "If there were originally no bondage, who would seek liberation? is an explanation by way of affirmation (*anvaya*) to demonstrate non-duality; this eliminates the two dharmas.

"Without bondage there is no liberation, and thus there is neither delight nor aversion. This refutes and dispels the two emotions; since there is no liberation to be delighted in and no bondage to be averse to.
"This is called" concludes [the section].
In the thirtieth [section], “King Śikhi said” marks the person who speaks;
what follows clarifies that which is spoken.
The initial statement, “The two: the right path and the wrong path,” presents the two characteristics by way of contrast.
There are two general explanations:
first, according to practice; second, according to the teaching of the Dharma.
Regarding practice, there are three:
1. The contrast between the ordinary person and the sage:
The eight deviations of the ordinary person are called the "false path," while the eightfold right path practiced by all sages is called the "true path.
2. The contrast between the Great and the Small [Vehicles].
That which is elucidated by the Hīnayāna is called "deviant" because it is the view of a different vehicle, whereas that of the Mahāyāna is called "correct.
Third, the contrast between the phenomenal and the real:
conceptualization based on conditions is called deviant, while direct realization of reality is called correct.
The same applies to practice.
Regarding the "approaching the Dharma," there are also three kinds:
first, external dharmas are called "false," while the Buddha-dharma is "correct."
2. Lesser teachings are heterodox, while Great Teachings are orthodox.
3. False teachings are termed heterodox, while True Teachings are orthodox.
Now, we shall discuss this in terms of the Dharma.
Regarding these within the context of phenomena (*dharma*), according to the third explanation, they are called "two" because they consist of the two divisions of the heterodox and the orthodox.
Below this, these two are merged to constitute "non-two"; by simultaneously negating both aspects of duality, one arrives at non-duality.
First there is the analysis, followed by the conclusion.

Within the analysis, the statement "abiding in the correct, one does not differentiate between the false and the correct" means that grasping at phenomena through deluded sentiment is called abiding in a false path, while extinguishing delusion and realizing the truth is called abiding in the correct path.
If one speaks from the perspective of abiding in error according to deluded sentiments, there is the correct outside of the erroneous, and thus they are two in contrast to the erroneous;

if one speaks from the perspective of extinguishing delusion and abiding in the correct, there is no erroneous outside of the correct. Since the erroneous does not exist, the "correct" is likewise a deluded counterpart and cannot be called truly correct.
Because there is no falsity, one does not give rise to the discrimination that "that" is a false path;
because truth and falsehood are opposites, one likewise does not discriminate that "this" is the true path. The simultaneous relinquishing of these two marks is called abiding in non-duality.
The section beginning with "Apart from these two" cites [the preceding] to conclude it.
Within the thirty-one [sections], the first—"The Joyful One said"—identifies the person and presents their distinct discourse;
the following sections clarify what was taught.
"Reality and unreality—these two" refers back to these two characteristics.
In the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), things are false and thus called unreal; in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are called real.
Below, these two are merged to form non-duality; first they are distinguished, and then they are concluded as one.
In the first part of the "Discernment," it says: "Even one who sees reality does not see reality; how much less so one who does not? This briefly clarifies non-duality.
From the perspective of the unreal looking toward the real, if there were a real existing outside of the unreal, then in relation to the unreal, they would constitute a duality.
Speaking of reality according to reality, there is no unreality apart from reality; therefore, reality itself is devoid of its opposite.
Because reality is devoid of its opposite, those who perceive reality do not grasp at the characteristics of reality.
Since even reality is not perceived, how much less so non-reality?
When both of these are extinguished, it is called "non-duality.
The section beginning with "The reason why" provides the explanation; first, there is a formal inquiry.
What is the intent of this question?
Since one is called "one who sees reality" (yathābhūta-darśin) because of seeing reality,
once it has been stated that one "sees reality," for what reason is it said that one does not see reality or what is non-real?
The following explains this in contrast [to the previous point]:
"It is not seen by the fleshly eye, but can be seen by the wisdom-eye" (cakṣur na māṃsacakṣuṣā dṛśyate prajñācakṣuṣā tu śakyate draṣṭum), which explains the aforementioned "actual seeing.
There are five kinds of eyes, each with its own distinct object of perception:
First, the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) perceives coarse and proximate forms within the manifest realm.
Second, the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) perceives subtle and distant forms beyond the manifest realm.

Third, the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) perceives the numerical categories of all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing—such as suffering and impermanence—as well as the faculties, inclinations, and dispositions of sentient beings.
Fourth is the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which sees that all phenomena are empty.
Fifth is the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*), which sees the true nature of phenomena.
Now, it is taught that emptiness is taken as reality; therefore, this reality is not seen by the fleshly eye.

Only the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) sees; even the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) and the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) do not see emptiness. This is discussed in contrast to the first [eye], which is why it is specifically stated that it is not seen by the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
"Yet this wisdom-eye neither sees nor does not see" explains the previous brief statement that one does not even see the real, let alone the unreal.
What is the meaning of this?
When a Bodhisattva’s eye of wisdom perceives emptiness, it exhaustively reaches the ultimate limit of emptiness and does not perceive an eye existing outside of emptiness that is able to see.
Since there is no eye existing outside of emptiness that is able to see, could there be an emptiness existing outside of the eye that serves as the object seen?

Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, through the clear realization of Mahāparinirvāṇa, does not perceive empty space; this very non-perception is called 'seeing emptiness,' and it is termed 'there is nothing that is not seen.'"
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Only those with the wisdom-eye can see it.
To see in this manner is to have no seeing as seeing; therefore, it is called 'seeing'."
It is similar to this.
Regarding these words of correct interpretation, one does not yet see the reality; it is easy to understand that one does not see what is unreal, so that need not be discussed.
One who sees the unreal is unable to see emptiness; this is called "not seeing."
When a bodhisattva severs and detaches from this mind of non-seeing, it is called "non-non-seeing.
The phrase "This is" below serves as the conclusion.
Thus far, in the first section, Vimalakīrti has posed the question, and the bodhisattvas have used words to dispel conceptual marks regarding their non-duality.
From here begins the second section, in which various bodhisattvas pose questions and Mañjuśrī responds by using words to dispel words, thereby manifesting non-duality.
Within this, first comes the question:
"Thus, these bodhisattvas," which introduces the persons who ask the question.
"Having each spoken thus" concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.
From "He asked Mañjuśrī" onwards is the formal presentation of the questions.
From "What kind of bodhisattva enters the gate of non-duality" onwards is Mañjuśrī’s response.
"In my own view," Mañjuśrī declares that his words follow his own intention and do not follow others.
"Regarding all phenomena, there is no verbal expression," and so forth, correctly elucidates their characteristics.
There are two kinds of dharmas:
first, the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and second, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Generally speaking, both of these possess meanings that can be expressed and meanings that cannot be expressed.
Phenomena are subsumed by names, and phenomena follow along with names; thus, everything is expressible.
Because they are expressible, the Buddhas always rely upon the two truths when teaching the Dharma.
Yet, when sought through ultimate reality, all phenomena are devoid of names.
Because they are nameless, all things are ineffable.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "All dharmas are free from verbal expression and free from the nature of conventional designations."
Within this, there is a further distinction: while the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) can be spoken of, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is ineffable.
Thus, Nāgārjuna said: "The ultimate truth is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases."

Now, based on the final section, within the "Gate of Distinguishing Characteristics," it is explained that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is wondrously quiescent and beyond words; therefore, it is said that the absence of verbal expression, up to the point of being free from giving answers, constitutes true non-duality.
Question: What is the difference between verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) and indicative consciousness (*vijñapti*), such that the latter is said to be non-existent? Answer:
To orally express written characters is called "speech" (*vāc*); to elucidate the Dharma through speech is what is termed "exposition" (*deśanā*).

Alternatively, to apply words in accordance with the Dharma is "speech," while to elucidate the Dharma through such speech is designated as "exposition. To manifest the Dharma by relying on a person is called "demonstration" (*nidarśana*), and to teach others to understand the Dharma through exposition is termed "making known" (*vijñapti*).
These exist according to worldly convention, yet in ultimate reality they are entirely non-existent; thus it is said that there is no speech, up to and including no cognition.
Since verbal expression is absent, the relationship between question and answer is severed; therefore, it is "beyond questioning and answering."
The phrase "This is" below serves as the conclusion.

Although the preceding bodhisattvas have dispelled marks (*nimitta*), they still leave behind words and dharmas, which constitute duality; only when words are extinguished and the absolute is realized is there non-duality (*advaya*). Therefore, it is now concluded that the absence of verbal expression and so forth constitutes entry into non-duality.
From this point downward is the third section, in which Mañjuśrī poses questions and Vimalakīrti reveals the truth through silence.
Within this, Mañjuśrī first initiates the inquiry, Vimalakīrti subsequently remains silent, and following the words "Mañjuśrī," there is another eulogy to further manifest it.
At the beginning, "Mañjuśrī" identifies the person who poses the question;
"Questioning Vimalakīrti" introduces the subject of the inquiry;
and "We have finished speaking" concludes the preceding section and introduces what follows.
"Virtuous one, what do you always say?"—the following passage is the formal statement of the question.
Next, Vimalakīrti reveals it through silence.

Vimalakīrti has thoroughly realized the reality of non-duality; in that state of reality, all affective states have ceased and all verbal expression is absent; therefore, he reveals it through silence.
Furthermore, while the previous Mañjuśrī spoke in response to establish the path, he was not yet equal to Vimalakīrti’s profound silence in relinquishing seeking.
Since the path is beyond words, he remained silent and did not speak.

The wordless path cannot be fathomed through speech; wishing to cause those who speak to cease their speaking so that they may meet in common realization, Mañjuśrī subsequently sighed to manifest this.
“Mañjuśrī sighed” serves as the general heading.
“Excellent, excellent! is precisely the expression of praise.
Because one transcends words to enter reality and manifest the most supreme principle, it is called "excellent" (śobhana).
The particle "zai" (哉) is an expletive used here to express the ultimate degree of excellence; the repetition of the word serves as an exclamation praising its goodness.
The passage beginning with "down to the point that there are no words or letters" sets forth the specific nature of this goodness.
Transcending speech and reaching ultimate silence, it is therefore said "even unto.
Speechlessness is itself the Way; the Way transcends verbal opposition. For this reason, it is called "truly entering non-duality."
The preceding section first clarifies the entry into non-duality; the following section clarifies the benefits of the teaching.
Five thousand bodhisattvas all entered into non-duality and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Chapter 10: The Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation (Four Editions). Regarding the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation": this chapter relies upon the Tathāgata Fragrant Accumulation to manifest the fruit of the pure lands of all Buddhas. The title of the chapter is named according to the person upon whom it relies, thus it is called the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation."
Within this chapter, there is a threefold analysis: first, the subject matter to be determined;
second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; and third, the exegesis according to the text.
Regarding the subject matter to be determined, there are two parts:
First, the classification according to the manifestation of Vimalakīrti’s virtues.

This chapter also serves to reveal the inconceivable virtues of Vimalakīrti; taking the fragrant food from the Accumulated Fragrance World and the vast containment within a small room are the manifestations of his inconceivable virtues.
Second, the analysis according to the Dharma.

"Dharma" refers to the causes and effects of the Dharmakāya and the Pure Land. Here, the text specifically clarifies the causes and effects of the Pure Land: the wondrous adornments of the World of Universal Fragrance are explained as the fruit of the Pure Land, while the cultivation of the ten and eight practices mentioned in the subsequent text are explained as the causes of the Pure Land.
The analysis is thus completed.
Next, the purpose of this exposition will be explained by returning to the two meanings previously mentioned.
First, regarding the intention behind [the title] as explained through Vimalakīrti:
among the four pairs of distinct meanings within Vimalakīrti’s virtues, these have already been analyzed above.
The section beginning with "Entering Non-duality" constitutes the fourth pair.
Within this pair, that which was practiced in the preceding chapter constitutes the actualization through cultivation;
that which is accomplished in this chapter constitutes the attainment of the virtue of inconceivable liberation.
Since there is a distinction between the causal practice and its fruition, it is necessary to differentiate them.
Furthermore, while the preceding chapter on "Entering the Gate of Non-duality" clarified the essence of liberation, this chapter clarifies its function.
Since function arises based upon the essence, it is explained next.
Second, the purpose of the discourse is explained by way of the Dharma.

From the preceding sections, it has been extensively clarified how kings, ministers, and others come to inquire after the Illustrious One’s illness in order to understand the causes and effects of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya;
this chapter clarifies the two types of pure causes and effects of the Buddha.
Since the body must necessarily rely upon the land, it is necessary to discern this.
Such is the intent of its introduction; now, its text must be explained.
This chapter consists of two parts:
I. The correct exposition of the Dharma;
II. From "Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī among the great assembly" onwards, the clarification of the benefits of the teaching.
Within the former, there are further two parts:
1. First, by taking up the fragrant food as the cause for mindfulness of Śāriputra, the fruit of the Pure Land is clarified.

2. From the passage beginning with "Those bodhisattvas, having heard this, all said, 'Not yet,'" down to the point where they praise and request [the teaching], the causes of the Pure Land are clarified.
Regarding the fruit of the Pure Land, the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) is most prominent; it is cited as a marvel to illustrate its excellence.
Regarding the cause of the Pure Land, the Sahā world is clearly superior; therefore, the explanation is given here.
Thus, the causes and fruits of the Pure Land elucidated herein fulfill the first assembly.
How is this established?

In the first assembly previously, it was proclaimed that when a bodhisattva attains buddhahood, they possess a land endowed with all merits; however, its characteristics were not yet fully revealed. Now, by resorting to the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha), these are made manifest; thus, in the subsequent text, it is clarified that in the Land of Universal Fragrance (*Saṃghāṭa*), everything is made of fragrance—such as the towers, pavilions, walkways, fragrant grounds, groves, and gardens, all being of such a nature.

Furthermore, in the first assembly, it was proclaimed that when a bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings of the Mahāyāna will come to be born in his land; however, as their characteristics were not yet fully revealed, they are now clarified through the example of the Land of Fragrant Accumulation. Thus, in the subsequent text, it is made clear that in the Land of Fragrant Accumulation there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only pure devas and bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, in the first assembly, it was proclaimed that when a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings endowed with all merits will come to be born in his land; yet at that time, their marks were not yet manifest.

Now, this [state] is also manifested by way of relying upon the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha); therefore, in the subsequent text it is explained that the bodhisattvas of the Land of Fragrant Accumulation obtain the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues (Sarvaguṇakośa) as soon as they are born beneath the fragrant trees, and that all the merits possessed by bodhisattvas who have attained this samādhi are fully complete.
The results are thus.

Furthermore, in the previous assembly, the practices of the six perfections and the four means of integration were proclaimed as the causes for the land, yet their specific locations were not clarified; they are now distinguished here. Therefore, in the following text, it is explained that the Sahā world alone possesses ten features that do not exist in other pure lands.

Furthermore, in the previous assembly, it was proclaimed that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the causes for the Pure Land, yet the specific dharmas were not explicitly set forth; they are now being elucidated here. Therefore, in the following text, it is clarified that when this bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, their conduct remains free from blemish or flaw, and they are born in the Pure Land.
These eight [chapters] consist entirely of methods for gathering and clarifying; by relying on these gatherings, one gives rise to all practices as causes for the Pure Land.
Such are the causes.

Regarding the initial clarification of the fruit of the Pure Land: first, Śāriputra’s thought regarding food serves as the occasion, and subsequently, Vimalakīrti takes food for him, manifesting his own inconceivable power and revealing the matters of the Pure Land of Fragrant Accumulation.
Regarding "recollection of the relics" (*śarīra-anusmṛti*): the phrase "in these relics" refers to the person who gives rise to the recollection.
Because this wisdom is superior and capable of producing many [beneficial effects], one specifically generates this recollection.
He then gave rise to this thought:
"The time for the meal is approaching; where do these bodhisattvas always eat?
It was because the room was still empty that he conceived this thought.
It is precisely because food and drink are necessities at all times that one contemplates them.
Furthermore, because the contemplation of food gives rise to many insights, one now contemplates it.
