Among those who eat, there is the practice of begging for food; therefore, he did not do so.
Furthermore, because his previous thought of sitting was intended for his disciples and yet resulted in his being rebuked, he did not raise it now.
Regarding the section where Vimalakīrti goes down to fetch food, there are three textual divisions:
first, he rebukes what [Śāriputra] was thinking, commanding him to abandon the impure food;
second, from "If you wish" onwards, he grants permission to fetch a drink and instructs him to seek pure food.
III. From "At that time, Vimalakīrti entered samādhi" onwards, he formally went to fetch food to fulfill his intention.
At the beginning, "Vimalakīrti" is mentioned to introduce the one who enters [samādhi] and delivers the rebuke.
"Knowing their humble intent" clarifies the reason for the reprimand.
"And spoke," and so forth, correctly presents the words of the reprimand.
"The Buddha has taught the eight liberations; you, O worthy ones, should receive and practice them" cites what was clarified.
The eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) are the methods for transcending desire; thus, they are singled out for mention.
Their meaning is as explained in other chapters and should be discussed in detail there;

for now, their names shall be listed. These are: first, possessing the perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms; second, lacking the perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms; third, the liberation through the perception of purity; fourth, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); fifth, the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); sixth, the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); and eighth, the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).
These eight [liberations] are free from bondage and are thus called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).
Because they turn their backs on and depart from lower faults, they are termed "turning away" (*prātikūlya*) in the sūtras.
Furthermore, Nāgārjuna says: "To turn one's back on the five objects of desire and abandon the mind of attachment is also called 'turning away'."
"Virtuous one, you accept and practice [this]" clarifies that one should be free from desire.
"How could there be any admixture of desire? and so forth, is a reprimand based on this clarification.
"How could it be permissible? means "how could it be right?"
If one practices the eight liberations, can one still partake of the food of sensual desire while listening to the Dharma?
Because there are many faults in consuming such defiled food, it is censured and one is urged to abandon it.
Question:
Previously, Śāriputra was mindful of food for the sake of the bodhisattva; why then did Vimalakīrti reproach him for his own desire?
Answer: [The commentary] says:
When Śāriputra previously contemplated food, it originally arose from his own mind that he must eat.
Because he himself had desires, he thought that others must have them as well; therefore, he wondered what the Bodhisattva always eats.
Vimalakīrti has now deeply examined their fundamental nature and therefore rebukes them.
From this point on, the second section permits him to take food.
"If you wish to eat," he says, pointing out what is required.
"I shall always cause you to obtain food such as you have never experienced before," he said, consenting to go and fetch it for him.
The food of the Pure Land brings manifold benefits when consumed; because he wished to cause [the boy] to seek it, he had to grant his permission.

From this point downward is the third section, which properly concerns the taking of food; it demonstrates one's own inconceivable power to lead others to practice and study, while simultaneously manifesting the fruit of the Land of Universal Fragrance to inspire people’s aspiration for it.
In this passage, the thesis is to manifest purity by contrasting it with impurity.
The text consists of six sections, which can be condensed into three pairs. Regarding these six sections:
first, Vimalakīrti, through his supernormal powers, reveals the realm of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa from the upper direction and dispatches others to fetch food, so that the assembly may behold it.

2. From "Those great beings, having seen the transformation" onwards, it clarifies that the bodhisattvas and others from the Land of Universal Fragrance, having traveled there due to the transformation, came to hear the Dharma after coming to know this Sahā world.
These two pairs demonstrate different lands so that they may know one another.
Third, from "Vimalakīrti then transformed nine million [beings]" onwards, it clarifies how this small room in the Sahā world can contain such vast space.
4. From "Vimalakīrti tells Śāriputra and the others that they may eat" onwards, it clarifies how a small amount of food from the realm of Universal Fragrance suffices for all.
These two sections form a pair, demonstrating extraordinary events so that they may respect one another.
5. From "Vimalakīrti asks the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa what he teaches" onwards, the text reveals the manner in which that Tathāgata gathers others.
6. From "Those bodhisattvas ask Śākyamuni what he teaches" onwards, it clarifies the method by which this World-Honored One opens the path.
These two pairs display distinct dharmas for mutual study.
Among the six, the first four are intended to manifest the benefit of food, while the latter two sections are intended to manifest the benefit of the Dharma.

Within the section on the benefits of eating, there are four parts: first, Vimalakīrti takes [the food]; second, that Buddha gives it; third, Vimalakīrti receives the food from another; and fourth, Vimalakīrti gives it to the assembly to eat.
The beginning and middle sections consist of three parts:
first, Vimalakīrti manifests the realm of various fragrances so that this assembly may see it;
second, from the passage "He asks the bodhisattvas" onwards, he commands the assembly to take the food.
3. Regarding the passage beginning with "At this, Vimalakīrti did not rise from his seat," he commands the assembly that they shall not obtain [the food] and dispatches others to go and fetch it.
Within the first section, Vimalakīrti first appears, and subsequently the entire assembly beholds him together.
Question: For what reason did Vimalakīrti manifest himself there so that the assembly might see him?
It was to reveal the Pure Land, so as to cause the assembly to seek it.
Furthermore, he manifests his own inconceivable power in order to cause the multitude to learn.
How does he manifest it?
There are two types of distinctions:
First, it is to demonstrate that what is apprehended is real and not illusory, employing the real to manifest inconceivable power;
second, it is to demonstrate that what is apprehended is distant and not near, employing the distant to manifest inconceivable power.

In the text, the initial statement "immediately enters samādhi" indicates that the basis for manifesting transformations is never absent; he enters [samādhi] in accordance with each manifestation, employing his supernormal powers to display their function—this is the inconceivable power of mastery over psychic faculties (ṛddhividhi).
"Manifesting to the great assembly" refers to the purpose of the manifestation.
Below, that which is manifested is explained, and therein there are five parts:
first, indicating the directions and boundaries.
2. To indicate the distance: "passing through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers";
3. The land manifested: "the name of the land is Saugandhika";
4. The Buddha manifested: "the name of the Buddha is Gandhottama, who exists at present."
5. A detailed exposition of their characteristics based on what is manifested.
There are four aspects to this exposition of characteristics:
first, the land; second, the persons; third, the land; fourth, the persons.
"The fragrance of that land is the foremost among all the ten directions" constitutes the first section, clarifying the excellence of the land.
Generally speaking, there are three kinds of adornments in a Pure Land, as already distinguished above:
first, the adornment of phenomena (*vastu-vyūha*), consisting of the exquisite and superior five sensory desires;
Second, the adornment of the Dharma, which exclusively expounds the Mahāyāna;
third, the adornment of persons, which consists solely of bodhisattvas.
These three adornments are all possessed by the various fragrances; this constitutes the "fragrance-adornment" within the first category, the "adornment of things."

"In that land there are no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; there are only assemblies of pure great bodhisattvas, for whom the Buddha preaches the Dharma. This second section clarifies the excellence of the people.
This also constitutes the adornment of the person and the Dharma.
“In that realm, all are towers made of fragrance” is the third section, which again clarifies the excellence of the land.
“That Buddha, together with... and following is the fourth section, which again clarifies the excellence of the person.
"The Buddha and the bodhisattvas are currently sitting together to eat" indicates that the recipients of the offerings are superior.
"There are various sons of gods, all named Fragrance," and so forth, indicates that those capable of making the offerings are superior.
The manifestation of the land above has been such that it can be known by all who see it.
From here on, the second section concerns the summoning of the assembly to take food.
Why not bypass the true assembly and instead dispatch a transformation-body to fetch the food; why must the assembly itself be summoned?
This is to demonstrate that he does not exalt himself nor disparage the assembly.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to manifest his own superior power in contrast to them, so as to cause the assembly to develop respect and aspire for Buddhahood.
Within this, there are four parts:
1. Vimalakīrti commanded the assembly to take food; therefore, he asked the bodhisattvas, "Virtuous ones, who among you can bring that Buddha’s meal?
This refers to the act of transporting or carrying it on a palanquin.
2. "Because of Mañjuśrī’s majestic spiritual power, the assembly remained silent.
Mañjuśrī, acting as an emissary to transform and gather [the disciples], caused them to be silenced.
Mañjuśrī, with what intention do you wish for Vimalakīrti to dispatch an emanation to fetch [the flowers]?
Once Vimalakīrti’s emanation has gone, many bodhisattvas there will follow that emanation, inquiring about its origin, and come here to listen to the Dharma.
There is no propriety in others proceeding further; therefore, he established the rule that they should remain silent.
Third, Vimalakīrti struck the assembly and ordered them to take [the food].
That many virtuous and benevolent ones were unable to take the food is indeed very clear.
Therefore, he now strikes back, saying: "For this great assembly to be treated thus by you would surely be a source of shame.
Fourth, Mañjuśrī explains the fault to the assembly:

"As the Buddha has said, 'Do not despise those who have not yet studied,' for sentient beings possess the virtue of learning toward liberation; they are unable to grasp it immediately, so I pray that you do not treat them with contempt or insult."
This concludes the third section: Vimalakīrti commands the assembly that they must not go [to fetch the food] himself, but instead sends a transformation-body (nirmāṇa) to retrieve it.
Why does he not go in person, but rather employ a transformation?
Vimalakīrti is the master of this transformation-food; as a guest is present in his room, it is not appropriate for him to abandon them abruptly.
Furthermore, wishing to cause those bodhisattvas to seek out the transformation-body and infer its origin so that they might come here to hear the Dharma, he does not depart from his own body.
Within this, there are three aspects:
first, he transforms himself into a bodhisattva, with marks and signs of extraordinary excellence;
2. From "And he addressed him" onwards, it teaches the act of going to fetch the food;
3. From "At that time, the emanation" onwards, it clarifies how the emanated bodhisattva receives the command to go and fetch it.
At the beginning, the passage "Vimalakīrti did not rise from his seat but remained among the assembly before the meal" clarifies the place where the transformation occurs.
The passage "He manifested as a bodhisattva, with marks and signs, radiance, and superior majesty" clarifies what was produced by the transformation.
According to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, there are three types of the holy body (*āryakāya*):
first is the true body (*dharmakāya*), which refers to the dharma-body and the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*);
second is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which manifests births according to the needs of those to be transformed.
The third is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which arises from the response-body.
Now, Vimalakīrti is fully endowed with these three bodies:

the essence of Vimalakīrti’s true virtue is the true body (*dharmakāya*); that which he receives in Vaiśālī is the response-body (*sambhogakāya*); and the bodhisattvas whom he transforms are the transformation bodies.
In the second instruction, the phrase "and addressed him, saying" summarizes the words of the teaching.

What follows below explains them in detail: first, it indicates that one must go in person to the place where the instruction is required; below that, it provides the words for requesting [the precepts].
The phrase "As my words say" generally summarizes the instructional language.
Below, it is treated specifically; therein, first, he is instructed to inquire after the World-Honored One’s well-being.
From the words "I wish to obtain" onwards, he is instructed to seek food.
The passage beginning with "Now, this joy" clarifies the purpose for which the alms are sought.
"Causing those who delight in the small [vehicle] to attain the vast Great Way" refers to the benefit of the Dharma;
"also causing the fame of the Tathāgata to be heard everywhere" refers to the benefit of transmitting it to others.
Furthermore, by propagating the Great Way, one receives the benefit of the Dharma;
likewise, by causing the fame of the Tathāgata to be heard everywhere, one receives the benefit of hearing of the Buddha.
It is asked:

Why is it that Śāriputra’s mindfulness of food was directed specifically toward the bodhisattvas, while Vimalakīrti’s taking of food was directed specifically toward those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle?
Answer:
Śāriputra’s mindfulness of food was directed specifically toward the bodhisattvas; the meaning is as explained previously.
Furthermore, the Śāriputras truly believe that the bodies of bodhisattvas have things upon which they depend, and thus take food as their sustenance.

Vimalakīrti deeply knows that bodhisattvas have no such needs; his taking of food at this time is solely intended to allow those who delight in inferior teachings to behold the inconceivable and wondrous efficacy of the Buddha and bodhisattvas’ pure land realms, thereby inspiring them to resolve to seek enlightenment.

Regarding the third transformation of going to fetch food: first, the transformed Bodhisattva ascends to the upper regions so that the entire assembly may see him; subsequently, the transformed Bodhisattva speaks to seek food, and the entire assembly hears his words, which are exactly as previously instructed.
The first section above demonstrates the manifestation of the realm of various fragrances and the dispatching of emanations to fetch food, which all the assembly witnessed together.
From here on, the second section clarifies how the bodhisattvas and others in the Garden of Various Fragrances, having learned of this through the emanations, came to hear the Dharma.

Question: Since all Buddhas are identical and not different, one has already attained the Dharma heard from that Buddha; why then take the trouble to come here? Generally, there are three explanations: 1. To pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and to hear the Dharma. 2. To manifest the power of the Buddha’s spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). 3. To cause sentient beings who have not yet developed faith to do so. By seeing the Buddha’s arrival, those who have not yet believed will develop faith, and those who already believe will increase their faith. Furthermore, by hearing the Dharma, they will attain the path and fruit. Therefore, it is necessary to come here. This is the first explanation. Second, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the Dharma they preach is not the same. For example, Śākyamuni Buddha preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* in the land of Jambudvīpa, whereas the Buddhas of the ten directions preach various other sūtras. Thus, one must come here to hear this specific teaching. Third, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the assemblies differ. Here, the assembly consists of bodhisattvas, whereas in other lands the assemblies consist of śrāvakas. Therefore, one must come here to see the bodhisattva assembly. Fourth, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the time periods differ. Here, it is the age of the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*), whereas in other lands it may be a period of purity. Therefore, one must come here to see the world of the five corruptions. Fifth, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the manner of preaching differs. Here, the Buddha preaches the Dharma by means of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), whereas in other lands he may preach by means of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) or other methods. Therefore, one must come here to hear the Dharma of the six perfections. Sixth, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the Dharma gates differ. Here, the Buddha preaches the Dharma gate of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), whereas in other lands he may preach the Dharma gate of the existence of all phenomena. Therefore, one must come here to hear the Dharma gate of the emptiness of all phenomena. Seventh, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the teachings differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the Mahāyāna, whereas in other lands he may teach the Hīnayāna. Therefore, one must come here to hear the Mahāyāna. Eighth, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the practices differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the practice of the bodhisattva path, whereas in other lands he may teach the practice of the śrāvaka path. Therefore, one must come here to hear the bodhisattva path. Ninth, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the fruits differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the fruit of Buddhahood, whereas in other lands he may teach the fruit of arhatship. Therefore, one must come here to hear the fruit of Buddhahood. Tenth, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the causes differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the cause of the bodhisattva path, whereas in other lands he may teach the cause of the śrāvaka path. Therefore, one must come here to hear the cause of the bodhisattva path. These are the ten reasons for coming here. Furthermore, there are two further reasons: first, to show that the Buddha’s power is inconceivable; second, to cause sentient beings to generate the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). If sentient beings were to see that the Buddha’s body is vast and immeasurable, they would immediately generate the thought of enlightenment. Therefore, it is necessary to come here. This is the twelfth explanation. Finally, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the lands differ. Here, the land is made of gold, whereas in other lands it may be made of crystal, lapis lazuli, or other substances. Therefore, one must come here to see the golden land. This is the thirteenth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the adornments differ. Here, the land is adorned with seven kinds of jewels, whereas in other lands it may be adorned with other jewels. Therefore, one must come here to see the adornment of the seven jewels. This is the fourteenth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the retinues differ. Here, the retinue consists of bodhisattvas, whereas in other lands it may consist of śrāvakas. Therefore, one must come here to see the retinue of bodhisattvas. This is the fifteenth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the teachings differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the Dharma of the Great Vehicle, whereas in other lands he may teach the Dharma of the Small Vehicle. Therefore, one must come here to hear the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. This is the sixteenth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the times differ. Here, it is the time of the five corruptions, whereas in other lands it may be a time of purity. Therefore, one must come here to see the world of the five corruptions. This is the seventeenth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the ways of transformation differ. Here, the Buddha transforms himself into a human form, whereas in other lands he may transform into a celestial form. Therefore, one must come here to see the human transformation. This is the eighteenth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the methods of teaching differ. Here, the Buddha uses the method of the six perfections to teach, whereas in other lands he may use the method of the four foundations of mindfulness. Therefore, one must come here to hear the teaching of the six perfections. This is the nineteenth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the fruits differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the fruit of Buddhahood, whereas in other lands he may teach the fruit of arhatship. Therefore, one must come here to hear the fruit of Buddhahood. This is the twentieth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the causes differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the cause of the bodhisattva path, whereas in other lands he may teach the cause of the śrāvaka path. Therefore, one must come here to hear the cause of the bodhisattva path. This is the twenty-first explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the lands differ. Here, the land is made of gold, whereas in other lands it may be made of crystal, lapis lazuli, or other substances. Therefore, one must come here to see the golden land. This is the twenty-second explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the adornments differ. Here, the land is adorned with seven kinds of jewels, whereas in other lands it may be adorned with other jewels. Therefore, one must come here to see the adornment of the seven jewels. This is the twenty-third explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the retinues differ. Here, the retinue consists of bodhisattvas, whereas in other lands it may consist of śrāvakas. Therefore, one must come here to see the retinue of bodhisattvas. This is the twenty-fourth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the teachings differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the Dharma of the Great Vehicle, whereas in other lands he may teach the Dharma of the Small Vehicle. Therefore, one must come here to hear the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. This is the twenty-fifth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the times differ. Here, it is the time of the five corruptions, whereas in other lands it may be a time of purity. Therefore, one must come here to see the world of the five corruptions. This is the twenty-sixth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the ways of transformation differ. Here, the Buddha transforms himself into a human form, whereas in other lands he may transform into a celestial form. Therefore, one must come here to see the human transformation. This is the twenty-seventh explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the methods of teaching differ. Here, the Buddha uses the method of the six perfections to teach, whereas in other lands he may use the method of the four foundations of mindfulness. Therefore, one must come here to hear the teaching of the six perfections. This is the twenty-eighth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the fruits differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the fruit of Buddhahood, whereas in other lands he may teach the fruit of arhatship. Therefore, one must come here to hear the fruit of Buddhahood. This is the twenty-ninth explanation. Furthermore, although the Buddhas are identical and not different, the causes differ. Here, the Buddha teaches the cause of the bodhisattva path, whereas in other lands he may teach the cause of the śrāvaka path.
First, they come for their own sake.

They wish to make offerings to and listen to the Dharma from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas here, because through the most excellent conditions provided by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in this region, making such offerings and listening to the Dharma will bring them great benefit.
Second, they come for the sake of others.
There are two purposes:
first, so that the sentient beings of that land may encounter the most fundamental causes and conditions with this Buddha here, and thereby obtain benefit through seeing him.
Their power and virtue being weak and inferior, they are unable to move themselves and must be guided by great bodhisattvas.
Thus, those such as Anantakāya and Vairocanaprabha each brought immeasurable bodhisattvas here to obtain benefit.
Such are these [reasons].
Second, he comes for the sake of the sentient beings of this land.
The sentient beings of this land ought to see him come, so that they may obtain great benefit.
This is the second reason for coming for the sake of others.
Third, one must come in order to extol the merits of the Triple Gem.
Among these, there are those who extol the virtues of the Buddha, such as when he first attained enlightenment, or when the assembly of bodhisattvas gathered to offer praise, and so forth.
Or it may be to manifest the Dharma; the ways of manifesting the Dharma are manifold and cannot be listed in full.
Or it may be to extol the merits of the bodhisattvas; the meanings of these merits are not singular.
Now, as these bodhisattvas have come from the Land of Universal Fragrance, they must embody all these aforementioned intentions.
In this passage, the primary purpose is that they have come for their own sake and also wish to proclaim the virtues of Vimalakīrti.
There are five sections within the text:
first, the bodhisattvas from the Land of Universal Fragrance observe others posing questions, and the Buddha there provides detailed answers.
2. The Bodhisattva inquires closely: "How is it that this person, Vimalakīrti, is able to perform such a transformation?
That Buddha answers him in full detail.
3. That Tathāgata places fragrant food in his alms bowl and gives it to the transformed Bodhisattva.
4. The Bodhisattva Saṃghagandha requested to come here, and that Buddha granted his permission.
5. From the passage beginning "At that time, the manifested Bodhisattva, having accepted the bowl," it is shown that he and his assembly arrived here through the power [of the Buddha].
At the beginning of the discourse, the question is first posed and the Buddha provides the answer.
Within the question, the initial phrase "those great beings" identifies the questioners;
"seeing the manifested bodhisattvas" clarifies what they have observed.
"Desiring what has never been before," he marveled at its sublime excellence.
He then posed a question:
"From where has this superior person come? Thus he inquired about his origin.
"Where is this Sahā world located? asks regarding its location.
"What is meant by 'one who delights in meager dharmas'? asks regarding their conduct.
That land is not small; this is why he asks.

It was because the emanated bodhisattva previously requested that Buddha, wishing to perform buddha-work in the Sahā world, so that those who delight in the "small" might attain the vast Great Way, that he posed this question.
"Immediately questioned the Buddha" means requesting the Sage to provide a definitive answer.
Below, the Buddha answers him.
"The Buddha told him," is a general statement introducing the response.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The lower direction" and so forth, the answers are given individually according to the questions.
Within this section, from the start up to "the realm is named Sahā," the response addresses the question posed above concerning where the Sahā world is located.
"Saha" is a term from the Hu language; here it is translated as "Endurance.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* explains:
because the sentient beings of this land endure the three poisons and all afflictions, and the land is named after its inhabitants, it is called "Endurance."

"The Buddha's name is Śākyamuni; in this world of five turbidities, he expounds the teachings of the Way for the sake of sentient beings who delight in minor [dharmas]. This answers the previous question regarding what it means to "delight in minor dharmas."
Regarding those beings transformed by that Buddha in the evil world of the five turbidities who delight in the Lesser Vehicle, they are called "those who delight in the Lesser.

The passage beginning with "There is a bodhisattva there named Vimalakīrti" answers the previous question concerning where this superior person has come from, clarifying that he is a manifested being sent by Vimalakīrti.
First, the list enumerates Vimalakīrti’s abiding in the inconceivable, clarifying what he has attained;
"preaching for the bodhisattvas" elucidates what he does;
and "therefore he dispatches a transformation-body" manifests what he sends forth.

"By extolling my name and praising this land, you shall cause those bodhisattvas to increase their merit" clarifies the purpose of the dispatch, so that they may aspire to it; this is called "increasing merit."
From this point downward is the second section, in which those bodhisattvas definitively evaluate Vimalakīrti.
By asking, "What kind of person is he that he can manifest such a transformation? they inquire about the man.
By stating, "His power of virtue, fearlessness, and supernormal powers are such as these," they inquire about his virtues.
The Buddha answered him:
"The Buddha’s words are most great," which addresses the first question by praising the person's high status;
"He dispatches emanations to all the ten directions," which addresses the second question by extolling the vastness of his emanations.
Third: That Buddha takes a bowl filled with fragrant rice from among the many bowls and bestows it upon the transformed bodhisattva;
this passage is clear and may be understood as it stands.
From here on, the fourth section concerns the request by the Bodhisattva Sarvagandhasugandha for the Buddha to come to this world, and that Buddha’s granting of permission.
In the opening of the *Śrāvaka-parivarta*, there is first the invitation; the initial listing of those who invite constitutes the formal request.
The phrase "All raising their voices," etc., expresses the actual words of the request.
The passage beginning with "To make offerings to Śākyamuni and behold Vimalakīrti," etc., clarifies the purpose for which the request is made.
The Buddha granted permission,
saying, "You may go," thereby allowing him to depart.
He then provided instructions, first admonishing his body and subsequently admonishing his mind.
The body has two aspects:
first, the fragrance of the body as gathered through teaching.
From the words "There is no present" (*wu jin*) onwards, it clarifies that which is enacted by the teaching.
Seeing that they are stained by attachment, it is called "arousing delusive clinging.
Second, the instruction to discard one's original form.
From the words "Do not allow" onwards, this clarifies the purpose of the instruction.
To see the superior and feel dejected or withdrawn is called self-contempt and shame.
The instruction within the mind, "Furthermore, you must not harbor thoughts of disparagement or contempt toward them that create obstacles," is a direct exhortation to abandon such faults.
"To slight others, to obstruct the straightforward, and to fear and thus not enter" is called the notion of obstruction.
The section beginning with "The reason why" provides an explanation, first posing a question and then offering the resolution.
"The ten directions are like space" clarifies that the primordial reality is pure;
that the lands and so forth are like space does not mean they are non-existent like space.
"Furthermore, for the sake of others who are inferior, the purity is not fully manifested" clarifies the manifestation of impurity through transformation.
Furthermore, one may consider that all ten directions are like empty space, clarifying that their nature is pure.
The Buddha, in order to transform those of lesser capacity, does not manifest the entirety of this purity; rather, he clarifies that his retribution is pure.
That land is truly pure, yet it is not manifested for the sake of transformation. Therefore, do not treat it with contempt or harbor thoughts of obstruction.
This concludes the fifth section below, concerning the transformation [of the bowl] and how that assembly arrived through the power of reception.
"At that time, the transformed Bodhisattva received the bowl of rice," meaning his aspiration was fulfilled.
"He gave it to nine million [people]," meaning those he gathered were to his heart's content.
"Both receiving the Buddha’s majesty and the power of Vimalakīrti" clarifies the basis upon which they have come.

To distinguish between them: the bodhisattvas from the Land of Universal Fragrance receive the majesty of that Buddha, while the manifested bodhisattvas receive the power of Vimalakīrti; however, in a general sense, both meanings apply.
"He suddenly vanished from that world" indicates the swiftness of his departure;
"in an instant he arrived at Vimalakīrti’s house" indicates the speed of his arrival.
Because he relied upon the power of the Sage, he did not appear [to others], yet in an instant he arrived here.
That [text] says "suddenly" (*chāng hūrán*), while this says "in an instant" (*xūyù*); these terms refer to the same momentary interval.
The preceding five sections together constitute the second part.

From this point downward is the third section, which clarifies how Vimalakīrti accepts the food through his transformative power, and simultaneously reveals the inconceivable power of Vimalakīrti’s small room to contain such vast space, thereby causing the newly arrived bodhisattvas to develop deep reverence.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, Vimalakīrti miraculously transformed nine million lion thrones, as high and wide as those previously described, and had the newly arrived bodhisattvas sit upon them.
2. The transformed bodhisattvas received the food from Vimalakīrti with their hands.
3. It was clarified that the fragrance of the food universally perfumed Vaiśālī as well as the trichiliocosm.
4. Because the fragrance universally perfumed [the world], the multitudes gathered like clouds.
This is the benefit of the fragrant rice.
Within this, the first section clarifies the joy of smelling the fragrance, with the mouth exclaiming that such has never been experienced before.
In the section on the gathering of clouds, the first part clarifies the assembly of the multitude of people.
From "The Earth Deities" (*bhūmidevatā*) onwards, the remaining hosts gather like clouds.
First, among those from the human realm, their assembly is identified and enumerated; next, they enter the house; finally, what they see is clarified, as they rejoice and pay homage.
The following clarifies the subsequent dwelling; the rest may be understood by the assembly.
This concludes the third section.

From here on is the fourth: Vimalakīrti receives the food and invites the assembly to eat together, thereby manifesting how a small amount of food from the Fragrant Accumulation [World] becomes vast, causing them all to feel deep reverence.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the invitation to share the food, which demonstrates that the food is inexhaustible;
second, from "All those bodhisattvas and śrāvakas" onwards, the explanation of the bliss of the food-body, which reveals the excellence of the food.
Previously, he had announced to all those seated—both great and small—to eat, yet did not summon the bodhisattvas.
A question was asked:
"In the past, he addressed everyone present, regardless of their rank; why is it that now he specifically summons only the śrāvakas?"
There are four meanings to this explanation:
First, the previous instruction regarding mindfulness of sitting was common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and thus was addressed equally to all.
Now, this mindfulness of eating is specifically for Bodhisattvas; fearing that the Śrāvakas might not dare to accept the food, it is addressed specifically to them.
Second, because bedding and seating are required regardless of size, they are announced to all.
Regarding food, however, the Śrāvakas have a distinct procedure for begging; since there is no intention to eat what is taken at this time, it is specifically announced to them alone.

Regarding the third meaning: as for the previously mentioned seats reaching such extreme heights, these accommodate the physical stature of this person; it is necessary to instruct the Bodhisattvas to transform their bodies so that they may sit [upon them], and to instruct the Śrāvakas to prostrate to the Buddha before sitting, as this serves as a universal notification.
The food currently taken is very little and not much; the Śrāvakas, being narrow-minded, fear that it will be insufficient and lack the intention to eat, so for their sake he informs them.
The Bodhisattvas have broad intentions; they know that what is little will ultimately become much and do not worry about not eating, which is why he does not inform them.
Regarding the fourth meaning: previously, when taking seats, there was no distinction made between the great and the small, and thus it was announced beforehand.

Now, regarding this taking of food, it is said that those who delight in the Lesser Dharma can attain the Great Way; the intention behind the Buddhas providing food is likewise so. This is truly because the Śrāvakas are the primary recipients, and therefore it is specifically announced now, desiring to have them eat together, so that they may know the rice is inexhaustible and resolve to generate the aspiration for enlightenment.
The meaning is as follows.
The text contains three parts:
first, directly exhorting the śrāvakas to partake of the meal;...
2. Regarding his own fruit, as a śrāvaka he reflects that his food is meager; as one who transforms bodhisattvas, he manifests that his food is inexhaustible.
3. From the passage "Thereupon, the rice in the bowl satisfied the entire multitude" onwards, it demonstrates that his food is inexhaustible.
