The Buddha then questioned him directly, posing two questions and receiving two answers.
"Śāriputra," the Buddha said, "do you see what the Great Being has done? This was a question as to whether he had seen it or not.
It was because Śāriputra had previously gone with Mañjuśrī and had witnessed all that Vimalakīrti manifested through the śarīra; therefore, he now questioned him.
“Indeed, I have seen it,” Śāriputra replied accordingly.
"What do you think?"—this asks whether [the former] is superior or inferior.
"I behold it as inconceivable," etc.—Śāriputra provides the answer.
"Inconceivable" is a general praise that reveals its superiority.
"Beyond what the mind can conceive and beyond what measurement can fathom" is a distinct praise that reveals its excellence.
"Beyond what the mind can conceive" clarifies that it cannot be known by consciousness.
Mind, consciousness, and awareness are distinctions of the eye.
"Diagram" (tu) means to measure; because the mind-consciousness of ordinary beings cannot diagram or measure it, it is therefore called "that which is not diagrammed by the intellect."
"It cannot be measured" clarifies that it cannot be known through intellectual wisdom.
Because the sage’s wisdom and discernment cannot reach it, it is therefore called "that which cannot be measured."
From here on, the second section distinguishes the aforementioned fragrant food so that this assembly may know it.
This text is divided into four parts:
first, Ānanda’s questioning and the Tathāgata’s explanation for him.
Second, Śāriputra himself describes the fragrance of his own body;
Ānanda questions him closely, and Śāriputra answers in full detail.
Third, when Ānanda’s food from Vimalakīrti has been digested, Vimalakīrti explains it for him.
4. Ānanda’s Praise and the Tathāgata’s Confirmation.
At the beginning, Ānanda first asked to initiate the discourse:
"The fragrance I have now smelled has never been experienced before; what kind of fragrance is this?"
The Buddha explains for him:
"This is the fragrance from the pores of that bodhisattva.
In the second section, first Śāriputra himself describes the fragrance of his own body; next, Ānanda asks where it comes from, and finally Śāriputra provides the explanation.

"The Elder Vimalakīrti took the leftover food from the Buddha in the Land of Universal Fragrance; those who ate it in his house had their every pore emit such fragrance as this, and therefore my body is fragrant."
In the third section, there are two questions and answers.
First, Ānanda asks, "How long will the fragrance remain? and Vimalakīrti subsequently replies, "Until this food is digested."
Ānanda asked again, "How long will it take for this to be eliminated? Vimalakīrti replied.
Within this response, the first part answers by way of the perfection of practice (*caryā-guṇa*), and the latter part answers by way of the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
In the preceding discussion on conduct, the initial section was addressed from the perspective of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the statement, "The power of this food will not be digested until seven days have passed," because the karmic response of ordinary beings is meager, it lasts for only seven days.
Next, regarding the śrāvakas:

"Those who have not yet entered the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) and eat this food will attain entry into that stage before it is digested," which refers to those from the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) upward.

"Those who have entered the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) and eat this food will attain right liberation, after which it will be digested," refers to the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-phala).

Speaking here in terms of the greater [classification], "If those who have not yet resolved their minds (an-utpādita-citta) eat this food, it will be digested once they resolve their minds," refers to those from the stage of spiritual lineage (gotra-bhūmi) upward; this may also refer to the first bhūmi and above.
"Those who eat with the resolve [to attain enlightenment] obtain the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti)," which refers to those from the seventh stage upward.
"Obtaining the patience of non-arising until reaching the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), after which they digest it," refers to the tenth stage.

Having exhausted the study of the ten stages and completed a single lifetime, one immediately attains bodhi; therefore, this is called being "in the position of succession for one more life" (ekajātipratibaddha).
Thus far, we have clarified the duration of the process in terms of practice.
The following section concerns the severance [of defilements], first providing a simile and subsequently applying it to the teaching.
"For example, there is a medicine named 'Supreme Flavor'" and so forth establishes the simile to illustrate the food.
"This rice is likewise extinguished after all afflictions have been eliminated before it is digested" distinguishes the food as being analogous to the simile.
Question:
Is this food actually edible food, or is it always a dharma that is metaphorically designated as "food"?
The family of Muktika says that this is a dharma, metaphorically designated by the name "food."
If it were truly just rice, how could it be like this?
If such a phenomenon can occur, why would it be called extraordinary?
Only when food can manifest such power is it truly inconceivable.
Furthermore, the Dharma can be shown as shallow rather than deep;
that food and drink can be shown is what constitutes the ultimate depth.
To take what is truly deep as shallow and seek a further depth elsewhere is to enter it erroneously.
All the objects of experience enjoyed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise like this; they can support spiritual practice and application, not merely this food.
It is like the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) born to a Wheel-Turning King: when the Holy King sits upon it, he naturally becomes free from desire and attains the four *dhyānas*;
even though he beholds the celestial maidens, it is as if he were looking at a Buddha-image, and no defilement of desire arises.

How much more so for the spheres of experience experienced by a bodhisattva, as it is said in the sutra: "A bodhisattva possesses a crown that illuminates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); when this crown is mastered, the natures of all phenomena appear before the mind, and all things are likewise."
In the fourth section, Ānanda first offers praise.
He praises in general by saying, "Never before has there been...
Then he praises again with specific detail, stating, "...this fragrant meal thus performs the work of a Buddha."
The Buddha speaks below to confirm and complete this;
because what has been praised is thus appropriate, he seals it once more.
From here on, the second section concerns purifying the mental vessel of the assembly.
The defilements of the mind obstruct the reception of the Dharma; therefore, it must be purified.
There are three things to be purified: first, to purify the minds of the Bodhisattvas with various fragrances;
second, to purify the minds of the Śrāvakas like the *āmra* fruit.
When the Bodhisattvas from the Land of Universal Fragrance arrived and saw this place, they conceived a sense of inferiority; therefore, it was necessary to purify it.

Furthermore, the assembly of Śrāvakas within the Āmra grove had not yet witnessed the wondrous virtue and supernatural power of Vimalakīrti, and thus their veneration was not yet profound; for these two reasons, purification was required.
In this passage, first the minds of the Bodhisattva Saṃghagandha are purified;
from the words "Cease, Ānanda, for those who possess wisdom" onwards, the minds of the Śrāvaka Āmra are purified.
In the first part of the preceding section, it is clarified that the Dharma-gates of the various Buddhas and Tathāgatas differ, in order to eliminate any sense of disparagement toward them.

From the passage beginning, "Ānanda, you see how diverse are the lands and soils of the Buddha-fields," the true equality is revealed to engender a sense of profound respect, such that Śākyamuni is revered as being identical to those other Buddhas.
Furthermore, within the preceding section, it first clarifies that the Tathāgata’s gates of transformation differ.
From the phrase "This is called entering" onwards, it concludes by clarifying the benefits, enabling others to understand and enter so as to eliminate mental faults.
The preceding Chinese text contains fifteen distinct phrases.
The first states, "Ānanda, there are some buddha-fields where the Buddha performs his buddha-work through light," and so forth;
these fourteen distinct types represent the manifestation of the practice in accordance with reality.
Regarding the final phrase, "The eighty-four thousand gates of affliction perform the work of a Buddha," this is a manifestation through reverse action.
What are these eighty-four thousand afflictions?
Since no such passage has been seen, one must not speak of it rashly.
However, if one reverses the eighty-four thousand gates of liberation into eighty-four thousand afflictions, the meaning will then be understood.
What are the eighty-four thousand gates of liberation?
They are fully and extensively enumerated in the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*.
That true Bodhisattva, named King of Joy (*Priyarāja*), reflected within himself:
“By practicing which samādhi can one swiftly attain the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of the pāramitās, the various dhāraṇīs, the gates of liberation, and so forth?
Having thought this, the Buddhas each answered him accordingly, saying:
“There is a samādhi named ‘Comprehending the Root of All Dharmas.’”
By practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, one will swiftly attain the eighty-four thousand gateways to the perfections (pāramitās) and so forth.
What are these? He said:
The Buddha’s virtues comprise three hundred and fifty gates; within each gate, one cultivates the six perfections as causes, thereby resulting in two thousand one hundred perfections.

By employing these various *pāramitās* as antidotes to the afflictions of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍāyatana*), there come to be twenty-one thousand *pāramitās*.
Regarding the "four great elements," ordinary worldlings take these four—earth, water, fire, and wind—as their body.
The Noble Ones cultivate the various perfections to attain the pure Dharma-body and abandon those four great elements; this is termed "antidote.
As for the "six decays," because the six objects of the senses are great thieves that cause the decay and depletion of wholesome dharmas, they are called the six decays.
The Sage cultivates the various *pāramitās* and enters the realm of the Buddhas, abandoning those six sense objects; this is called "treating the six decays.
By employing these twenty-one thousand *pāramitās* to treat the four types of mental illness, there are thus eighty-four thousand [remedies].

What are these? There are twenty-one thousand remedies for the disease of excessive greed, twenty-one thousand for the disease of excessive hatred, twenty-one thousand for the disease of excessive delusion, and twenty-one thousand for those with an equal proportion of the poisons; thus, there are eighty-four thousand in total.
These afflictions drive sentient beings to wander incessantly through the six realms, undergoing suffering without end, for the most part emaciated by exhaustion.
When the Buddhas manifest their appearance, they gather and transform sentient beings; therefore, they perform the work of a Buddha by means of these very afflictions.
Since afflictions are thus, so too are karma and suffering;
these are omitted from the text for brevity.
The gates of transformation are immeasurable, and this has been cited merely as an illustration.
The preceding section has extensively set forth the various gateways of the Buddhas' transformation.
The following section concludes by indicating the benefits of this knowledge, enabling those bodhisattvas who have come here to enter into the middle way and eliminate mental constructs.
"This is called entering all the Buddha-dharma gateways" is the concluding statement.
Based on the detailed explanation provided above, this is termed "entry.
The following section demonstrates the benefits of such knowledge.
"A Bodhisattva who enters this gate" refers to the one who possesses the knowledge.
Next, we shall discuss the benefits.
There are two kinds of benefits:
first, the benefit of being free from discrimination regarding the Buddha-lands; second, the benefit of rendering equal respect to all Buddhas.

Regarding the first part of the middle section, the statement "If one sees all pure and excellent buddha-fields, one does not feel joy, nor does one covet them, nor does one become conceited," is without fault in its vision of purity.

Not feeling joy at the outset is called "not rejoicing"; not having covetous seeking in the middle, such as a partial desire to be reborn there, is termed "not coveting"; and finally, being free from pride is described as "not being conceited."
"If one sees all impure buddha-fields and does not regard them with sorrow, is not hindered by them, and does not sink into them," means that beholding the profound without error is as follows:

being without initial anxiety or fear is called "not sorrowing"; being without middle-level constraints or difficulties, remaining detached without giving rise to [aversion], is called "unhindered"; and while the body remains there, not conceiving thoughts of falling downward or sinking away is called "not sinking."
The following clarifies the benefits of maintaining respectful equanimity toward the Buddhas.

The phrase "merely giving rise to a pure mind toward all Buddhas" serves as a general heading to indicate that the stage of faith in the Buddhas is distinct; it is called a "pure mind" because one's practice is not impure.
Being free from defilement and purely pristine, it is therefore said to be "only" (but).
The phrase "with joy and reverence, this is unprecedented" reveals the prior purity and celebrates the Buddha’s skillful transformation; this is why there is such joy.
Because he values the Buddha’s power of transformation, it is said that he "reveres" him;
because he praises the rarity of the Buddha’s transformations, it is said that they are "unprecedented.

The statement, "The merits of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are equal, yet they manifest different lands for the sake of transforming sentient beings," brings forth the extraordinary matter of what he reveres.
The preceding first section clarifies how the Buddha transforms the disparaging minds of the assembly through his diverse manifestations.
From here on, the second section clarifies how the Buddha truly gives rise to a mind of profound respect in the assembly.
Within this, the initial part clarifies that the Buddha truly gives rise to a mind of equality toward all beings.
The passage beginning with "Therefore it is called Samyak" concludes by praising and manifesting its excellence, thereby engendering a sense of profound respect among the assembly.

In the preceding section on "equality," the statement, "Ānanda, you see that the lands of the various Buddha-fields have various degrees of emptiness and non-emptiness," establishes a metaphor to reveal the Dharma; this is precisely what clarifies the equality of the lands.
From the phrase "seeing thus" onwards, the text distinguishes the identity of the Dharma with its metaphors, thereby clarifying the nature of the Buddhas and others.

Within this section, the initial statement—"The form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas may vary in number, but their unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇaprajñā*) does not vary"—briefly elucidates the Buddhas and others; this specifically clarifies the realized gnosis (*jñāna*) of the Buddhas and so forth.
"Various kinds of the majestic marks of the Buddhas' form-bodies," and so forth; this specifically clarifies the Buddhas and others, and by extension, it also reveals their other virtues.
Within this, first there is the specific enumeration, and from "endowed with all... onwards is the summary.
Within this section, the first part clarifies the equality of the virtues of the body, while the latter part clarifies the equality of the lands and so forth.

Within the former, concerning the virtues of the body, the initial portion clarifies his own virtues, while the section beginning with "Great Compassion" clarifies his virtues for the benefit of others.
"His dignified deportment, his conduct, and his lifespan" further clarifies his personal virtue.
"Expounding the Dharma to instruct others" reiterates his virtue of transformation.
Within his personal virtue, there are five kinds of equality:

First, the physical body; second, majestic power; third, the primary and secondary marks; fourth, the spiritual lineage; fifth, from "precepts and concentration" downward, the clarification of meritorious qualities; the remainder can all be understood accordingly.
The above has clarified the assembly of those born through equality and their minds of equality.
Hereafter, the second section concludes by praising and manifesting the profound respect of the assembly born through excellence, who revere Śākyamuni as they do the Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation.
The three names were first established according to their dharmas, and subsequently presented to manifest their excellence.
Although the specific names are immeasurable, three types shall be illustrated for now.
"Therefore, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha"; this is translated as "Right, True, and Perfectly Awakened."
The three [qualities] are called "right" (*samyak*); "miao" means "true. Repeated three times, they are named "Right.
*Buddha* means "Awakened.
Regarding the phrase "named Tathāgata," this is the name for the Tathāgata; because he has come by means of the path of suchness to achieve perfect awakening, he is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, just as the Buddhas who come later are also called Tathāgatas, they are also called "Buddha.
This term "Buddha" is simply the name for a Buddha.
Because the merits of all Buddhas are equal, all of them are designated as Samyak-saṃbuddha and so forth, up to the name Buddha.
The following section clarifies its excellence.
This contains three parts:
first, the formal praise that clarifies its excellence.
If these three meanings were explained in full detail, Ānanda and his peers would be unable to receive them.
Second, having heard this, Ānanda was unable to retain it; he then conceived a sense of retreat and did not dare claim himself to be one of great learning.
Third, the Tathāgata’s consolation.
Within the preceding section on formal praise, the statement "If I were to explain the meaning of these three phrases in detail" clarifies that their meaning is vast.
The subsequent passage, "You have exhausted your lifespan through kalpas and could not receive it," etc., manifests the characteristics of that vastness.
In this passage, it is first clarified that Ānanda alone, despite having a lifespan of one kalpa, is unable to receive and uphold [the teachings].
From the words "Even if" onwards, it is hypothetically stated that even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were like Ānanda, with a lifespan of one kalpa, they still could not receive them.
The passage beginning with "In this way, Ānanda, the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas... cites the vastness of the Buddha's virtues to establish the reason why [the Dharma] cannot be upheld.
The phrase "Anuttara-bodhi is without limit" clarifies the vastness of the Buddha's essence (*buddhatva*).
"His wisdom and eloquence are inconceivable" clarifies the vastness of the Buddha's activity.
"Ānanda said to the Buddha that he did not dare to call himself one of great learning" constitutes the second phrase, wherein Ānanda withdraws from his own claim.
Having heard this, he was unable to accept the meaning of these three phrases, and thus gave rise to a regressive thought.
From "The Buddha told" onwards is the third phrase, the Tathāgata’s consolation.
"The Buddha told Ānanda: 'Do not give rise to a regressive thought'" is the direct calming of his mind.

The meaning of the Buddha’s teachings is vast and manifold, beyond the reach of the śrāvakas; therefore, they are unable to receive them. It is not because Ānanda has lost his capacity for hearing and retaining that he is unable to receive them.
You have already been told: do not give rise to thoughts of retreat.
The section below provides an explanation, beginning first with a formal inquiry:
"Why did you previously state that one cannot accept the meaning of the three propositions, yet now say that one should not give rise to thoughts of regression?"
The following passage explains this in response:

"In the past, I said that among the śrāvakas, you were the most learned, but not equal to a bodhisattva. This was because I stated that you were the most learned among the śrāvakas, rather than among the bodhisattvas; thus, although you possess great learning, you are unable to receive the merits of the Buddhas. This inability does not arise from a loss or decline of merit, but is simply an obstruction.
Therefore, I exhort you not to give rise to thoughts of retreat.
The preceding section has purified the minds of those newly arrived bodhisattvas;
next, I shall purify the minds of the śrāvakas within the Āmra grove, causing them to conceive a profound sense of reverence for Vimalakīrti.

Within this, first it clarifies that the śrāvakas cannot fathom the wisdom and virtue of Vimalakīrti, and subsequently it reveals that the two vehicles cannot replicate the supernatural powers possessed by Vimalakīrti.
Regarding the former, the initial statement "Cease, Ānanda" halts his previous words.
It can also halt the mind that seeks to fathom [the Buddha's nature]; therefore, it says, "let it cease for now.
The following provides a formal admonition:
"Those who possess wisdom should not attempt to limit the Bodhisattvas," clarifying that such persons are unfathomable.

The passage beginning with "The height of all oceans may be measured" and so forth clarifies that the virtues of the Bodhisattva are immeasurable; it specifically mentions the Bodhisattva to correctly discuss Vimalakīrti.
In the subsequent section clarifying that supernatural powers cannot be fabricated, the phrase "you should set aside the conduct of Bodhisattvas" excludes the aforementioned practices.
The passage beginning with "This supernatural power manifested by Vimalakīrti at one time" etc., specifically clarifies that [others] are unable to perform such feats.
The phrase "this Vimalakīrti" refers to an inferior person.
"Manifested at one time" refers to the duration of the time.
"All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" and so forth clarifies the abundance of people.
"Throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas" refers to the length of the time.
If many people over many eons are still unable to accomplish it, how much less could a few people in a short time possibly do so?
The preceding section was the second [part], purifying the mental vessel of the assembly;
from here on begins the third [part], the formal instruction through the Dharma.
This section is divided into two parts:
everything up to this chapter constitutes the first part, and the "Chapter on Seeing the Multitude" (*Saṃdṛśya-parivarta*) constitutes the second part.
Within these two parts, there is a threefold analysis:
First, distinguished by way of conceptual differentiation:
this chapter transforms and benefits the Bodhisattvas of the Fragrant World, while the subsequent chapter transforms and benefits the multitudes of the Sahā world.
Second, distinguished by way of cultivation.

This chapter clarifies that which is cultivated within one's own stage, while the subsequent chapter reveals that which is practiced for superior progress; through such cultivation and practice, one enters the higher stages and is able to perceive the Buddha upon reaching the realm of Buddhahood.
Third, the analysis according to the Dharma.
"Dharma" refers to cause and effect; this chapter elucidates the cause, while the subsequent chapter elucidates the effect.
Within this chapter, there are three distinct textual sections:
I. The Bodhisattvas of the Land of Universal Fragrance request the Dharma and return to their land;
II. From "The Buddha said" onwards, the Tathāgata expounds the teaching for them;
III. From "At that time, those Bodhisattvas, having heard... onwards, it clarifies how the Bodhisattvas, rejoicing upon hearing the Dharma, pay homage and take their leave.
Within the initial request, there are two parts: first, the confession of prior transgressions;
from "Thus it is" (*evam astu*) onwards, the request for the subsequent Dharma.
Regarding the confession of prior transgressions, the phrase "At that time, in the world-system of Universal Fragrance" (*tadā saṃghagandhā lokadhātuḥ*) identifies and enumerates those individuals.
"Joining my palms toward the Buddha," he addresses those he has invited.
"I see that in this life I have harbored inferior thoughts," thus confessing his own transgressions.
"Today I repent and reproach myself," thereby relinquishing such thoughts and feeling remorse for his past faults.
The passage beginning with "For what reason? summarizes the Buddha’s previous teaching to clarify the basis for his repentance.

He states: "The skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas are inconceivable; they manifest different Buddha-lands in order to deliver sentient beings. Previously, I did not know this and falsely gave rise to discrimination; therefore, I now reproach myself.
In the procedure for making a formal request (*adhyeṣaṇā-dharma*), the phrase "Yes, indeed" (*evaṃ bhadanta*) is used to seek the Buddha’s permission.
"Evaṃ" (yes) carries the sense of exclusivity, while "bhadanta" (indeed) carries the sense of acceptability.
Because one exclusively seeks the Tathāgata’s acceptance of oneself, it is called "bhadanta."
"May you grant me a small portion of the Dharma" is a formal request for the Buddha to preach.
"When returning to that land, one should keep the Tathāgata in mind" clarifies the benefit of the Buddha's teaching.
Alternatively, these words may clarify that one’s own reverent compliance and mindfulness are derived from the Buddha’s grace.
To practice in accordance [with the Buddha] is called mindfulness of the Tathāgata; furthermore, to mindfully recollect the Dharma taught by the Buddha is also called mindfulness of the Tathāgata.
Below, the Buddha speaks for them.
Within this discourse, there are three parts:
First is the general exhortation:
"You should study the dharma-gate of liberation, which is both finite and infinite.
Second, from "What is it? onwards, the teaching is given according to specific details.
3. "This is the Dharma-gate of the Exhaustible and the Inexhaustible; you should study it. This concludes the exhortation to practice.
Regarding the initial summary, the term "the exhaustible" refers to that which can be conceptualized by worldly lords.
To speak of "inexhaustibility" means that the True Sovereign abides eternally.
The non-obstruction between these two is called liberation.
This passage sets forth its principle.
"You all should train yourselves" is the exhortation to practice;
the subsequent text provides the specific teaching.
Within this, the first part is a brief summary, while the section beginning with "Why not exhaust the conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) is the detailed exposition.
In the first part of the brief explanation, the statement "What is meant by 'exhaustion'? It refers to conditioned phenomena" explains what was previously mentioned regarding exhaustion.
Arising and functioning according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is termed "conditioned.
Because they are conditioned, these phenomena can be brought to rest; therefore, they are said to be "exhaustible."
"What is meant by 'inexhaustible' refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)," thus explaining the aforementioned "inexhaustibility.
Because the True Truth (*tattva*) is eternally abiding, it is called "unconditioned.
Because it is unconditioned, it cannot be extinguished; therefore, it is named "inexhaustible."
This commentary explains the aforementioned dharma-gate of liberation that is both exhaustible and inexhaustible.
From the passage "As a bodhisattva" onwards, it explains the learning of the Dharma by those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Generally speaking, there are three [aspects]:
1. The Gate of Grasping Quiescence:
Practicing in common with the śrāvakas, one does not dwell in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and does not depart from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
2. The Gate of Arising Activity.
Distinguishing it from the practices of the two vehicles, one does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Third, there is the perfection of dual cultivation:
one departs from the practices of the two extremes, neither dwelling in nor abandoning conditioned phenomena, and the same applies to the unconditioned.
When one does not dwell in the conditioned, one does not give rise to defiled attachment toward the conditioned;
when one does not abandon the conditioned, one does not give rise to fear toward the conditioned.
To be free from these two faults is called attaining liberation within the conditioned.
One does not abide exclusively in unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), nor does one cling to emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
one does not abandon unconditioned phenomena exclusively, nor does one fear emptiness.
To be free from these two faults is called attaining liberation within the unconditioned.

Now, this is for the sake of teaching the Bodhisattva Universal Incense (Samantagandha) how to give rise to function according to conditions; therefore, it is specifically granted and explained through the second gate.
The phrase "such as a bodhisattva" distinguishes [the bodhisattva] from the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
"Not exhausting the conditioned" refers to the *Bhūmi-sūtra*’s description of initiating superior practice that constantly accords with existence.
"Not dwelling in the unconditioned" refers to the *Bhūmi-sūtra*’s cultivation of the wisdom of skillful means, which does not abide in emptiness.
These two serve as gateways, which will be extensively elucidated below.

Within this, first, by means of the initial stage of practice, the meaning of neither-extinction-nor-abiding is clarified; furthermore, by means of the final completion of practice discussed below, its meaning of neither-extinction-nor-abiding is further explained.

In the preceding section, the meaning of not exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is first clarified, followed by the manifestation of the meaning of not dwelling in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Within the clarification of not exhausting the conditioned, there is first a question and subsequently a summary.
"What is meant by 'not exhausting'?"—this is the initial question.
"'Not being separated from,' etc."—this is the detailed exposition.
Since dharmas are manifold and difficult to discern, I shall now speak of them briefly.
The coarse division is twofold:
first, clarifying the mundane practices prior to the stages;
second, from "the cultivation of roots of goodness" (*caryā-prasthāna-kuśalamūla*) onwards, clarifying the supramundane practices of the [first] stage and above.
Within the practices of the world, one first initiates right cultivation;
with the passage "regarding all meditative concentrations as being like hell," one is taught to give rise to right cessation (*śamatha*).
Within the aforementioned right cultivation, one first teaches compassion and vows as the causal basis for practice.
The subsequent teaching concerns correct practice.
In the preceding teaching on the causes, the phrase "not departing from great kindness (maitrī) and not abandoning great compassion (karuṇā)" refers to the cause for benefiting others.
The use of "not departing" for kindness and "not abandoning" for compassion is merely a matter of phrasing from different perspectives.
"To never forget the aspiration for enlightenment" refers to the cause for the personal practice of the bodhicitta vow.
To resolve the mind to seek the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is therefore called "arousing the mind for omniscience."
"Sudden" refers to negligence.
To regard the bodhicitta as weighty rather than slight is called "not negligent";
to maintain it firmly without losing it is called "not forgetting."
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the lower teaching concerns right practice (*samyak-pratipatti*).

Within this, the initial section clarifies the practice of one’s own level (*svabhāga-caryā*), while the section beginning with "seeking the Dharma" clarifies the practice of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*).
In the preceding section on self-benefit, the practice of benefiting others was first clarified:
"Never becoming weary of teaching and transforming sentient beings" refers to the constant practice of transformation;
"constantly mindful of and acting in accordance with the four means of integration" refers to the practice of gathering through merit.
The following clarifies self-benefit.
"Upholding the True Dharma without sparing one's body or life" means steadfastly maintaining the True Dharma as the foundation of practice.
"Cultivating all roots of goodness without weariness" means practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
"Planting all roots of goodness" clarifies the cultivation of the sudden;
"having no weariness or fatigue" clarifies the cultivation of the constant.
"The will constantly abides in right dedication" means that by means of what has been cultivated previously, one seeks the Buddha above.
Seeking the mind without regression is called "abiding securely.
Skillfully employing all virtues to seek enlightenment is therefore called "skillful means of dedication.
These are the sequential stages for cultivating these three practices.
Within the section on "inferior advancement," wisdom comes first and merit follows.
Within the prior cultivation of wisdom, "seeking the Dharma without indolence" constitutes self-benefit,
while "expounding the Dharma without parsimony" constitutes benefit for others.
Within the subsequent cultivation of merit, "diligently making offerings to all Buddhas" constitutes one's own benefit (*svārtha*).
The following section on "fearlessness" and so forth constitutes the benefit of others (*parārtha*).
This consists of seven phrases.
First, "fearlessness toward birth and death" refers to the courageous mind; because one is fearless, one remains constantly engaged in teaching and transforming others.
There is also a sutra that says, "Entering into birth and death without fear," which has a similar meaning, though the translations differ.
Second, "having no sorrow or joy in the mind regarding all honors and insults" refers to an unshakable mind; because one is not moved by honor or insult, one is able to constantly transform others.
This is also the mind of equanimity, for through the absence of sorrow and joy, one is able to transform others with impartiality.

3. "Not slighting those who have not yet studied, but honoring those who study as if they were Buddhas" means being free from pride; because one’s mind is devoid of arrogance and haughtiness, one is able to receive and transform others.

4. "Causing those fallen into afflictions to give rise to right mindfulness" means the mind of guidance; it refers to teaching the cultivation of the six remembrances (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), and so forth, so that they may become free from afflictions.

5. "Not regarding the bliss of seclusion as noble" refers to following the mind of existence; because one does not prize the bliss of seclusion that is nirvana, one is always able to follow the cycle of existence to teach and transform sentient beings.
Sixth, "not being attached to pleasure" refers to the mind free from attachment.
Because one attains pleasure without attachment, one is able to relinquish it for the benefit of sentient beings.
Seventh, "rejoicing in that pleasure" refers to the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
The Bodhisattva focuses exclusively on benefiting others; therefore, he does not cling to his own pleasure, but instead transforms it into joy and celebration.
Thus far has been the first teaching on cultivating correct practice.
The instruction on rectifying the mind below consists of four parts.
First, the altruistic mind:

"Regarding all meditative concentrations as if they were hells" means that one distances oneself from the mundane mind; because one attains these states without relishing them, they are likened to hell.
"Contemplating saṃsāra as a garden": because one leaves behind the minds of the two vehicles and constantly delights in dwelling therein, it is like contemplating a garden.
Second, the mind of self-benefit.

"One should conceive the thought of a virtuous teacher toward those who come seeking [one's help]. One should give rise to a mind of reverence and joy; for just as a virtuous teacher instructs others to produce wholesome states, those who come to beg can likewise produce wholesome states within me, and are therefore regarded as teachers.

"Relinquishing all that one possesses while maintaining the perception of omniscience" gives rise to a mind of benefit and merit; because giving can produce the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), one rejoices without regret.
3. A further clarification of benefiting others:
"Seeing those who violate the precepts, one conceives the thought of rescuing and protecting them.
4. A further clarification of self-benefit.
“Regarding the various pāramitās as one’s parents” means they can give birth to the Dharma-body.
“Regarding the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas) as one’s kinsmen” means they can personally benefit oneself, and are thus like kinsmen.
The above clarifies mundane practices;
what follows clarifies supramundane practices, which are divided into two parts:
first, the cultivation of extensive practices.
The passage beginning with "With a mind courageous throughout countless kalpas of birth and death" clarifies the cultivation of supreme practices (*viśeṣa-caryā*).

Within the preceding section on extensive practice, the phrase "arousing roots of goodness without limit" means that one initially cultivates vastness; from the first bhūmi upward, one generates expansive vows and cultivates all practices, which is termed "arousing roots of goodness without limit."
Regarding the phrase "By means of all pure lands, one completes one's own land," this refers to the vastness of perfected practice.
Within this, there are four points:
first, the vastness of the retribution-gathering based on pure lands, which is expressed as "by means of the adornments of all pure lands, one completes one's own Buddha-land."
What is the meaning of this?

By extensively cultivating pure causes, one ensures that all causes for the adornment of sublime matters are fully present within one’s own land; therefore, it is said that "one completes one’s own Buddha-land through the acts of adorning various pure lands."
Second, based on the Pure Land, one gives rise to a sense of self-expansiveness and practices boundless giving.
There is also a sutra that speaks of "opening the gates for great giving," the meaning of which is similar.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are causes; for instance, take the case of giving (*dāna*).
Third, by relying on the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the maturation (*vipāka*) it encompasses is vast and extensive, being fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

Fourth, by relying on the Dharma-body, the causes from which it arises are vast and extensive: "Eliminating all evils, one purifies body, speech, and mind. All conditioned phenomena are causes; for instance, take the case of ethical discipline (*śīla*), as it is the most powerful among the practices that give rise to the primary and secondary marks.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "The undifferentiated causes of the thirty-two marks are all the observance of the precepts.
If one does not observe the precepts, one cannot even attain the body of a lowly person, let alone possess the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
The preceding section clarifies extensive practice; the following clarifies superior practice.
"With courage in mind throughout countless births and deaths, one’s resolve remains untiring upon hearing of the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues"—this arises from superiority.
The intentional mind possesses courage because it is capable of subduing and severing the sufferings of birth and death throughout countless eons.
It is called "unflagging resolve" because, having heard of the Buddha’s vast virtues, one resolutely practices without retreating.
"Prior intention" and "subsequent resolve" are synonymous terms for the eyes [of wisdom].
From the phrase "by means of wisdom" onwards, it concerns the excellence of the practice of setting forth.
Within this, there are two parts:
First, based on the aforementioned intention regarding birth and death, one possesses courage and initiates the practice of remedying faults;

second, from the term "unbreakable" (*abhedyā*) onwards, based on the aforementioned hearing of the Buddha’s resolve without weariness, one cultivates the practice of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgraha*).
Regarding the four phrases in the preceding section, the first two refute obstacles while the latter two encompass their remedies.

Within the former refutation of obstacles, the first uses wisdom to destroy the various afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and the latter uses diligence to subdue the armies of Māra and distance oneself from karmic hindrances (*karmāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, "destroying afflictions" clarifies the removal of the obstacle of non-liberation, while "subsequently crushing the demonic armies" clarifies the removal of the obstacle of practice.
Moreover, "destroying afflictions" clarifies the removal of the obstacle to wisdom, while "the demonic armies" clarifies the removal of the obstacle to merit.
In the first part of the preceding section, one first destroys one's own afflictions.
"Destroying the thieves of affliction with the sword of wisdom" refers to severing the causes of violating the precepts.
Wisdom is called a "sword" because it is capable of shattering [afflictions], and afflictions are metaphorically termed "thieves" because they inflict harm.
"Transcending the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases" refers to the fruit of the various precepts.
The following clarifies acting for the sake of others: "bearing the burden of sentient beings so that they may forever attain liberation.

Within this latter phrase, "subduing the armies of Māra with great diligence," *māra* refers to the four māras: the afflictions (*kleśa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), death (*mṛtyu*), and the celestial māra (*devaputra-māra*).
"Army" refers to the ten armies, as Nāgārjuna has explained.

Thus, his text states: "Desire is your first army; sorrow is the second; hunger and thirst are the third army; craving is the fourth; sleep is the fifth army; fear is the sixth; doubt and regret are the seventh army; anger is the eighth; the army of gain and honor is the ninth; and the dreamer at high noon is the tenth."
"By such armies as these, the renunciants are overwhelmed by dust; yet, through the power of my meditative wisdom, I shall destroy all your hosts.
Having attained the Way of the Buddha, I shall extensively liberate all beings.
One may also correctly designate the hosts of Māra as an "army" and cause them to be crushed and subdued through diligence.
The two preceding lines clarify the destruction of hindrances; the following two [lines] concern their subjugation and governance.

"Constantly seeking the wisdom of the true mark of non-conceptualization" corresponds to the first phrase above; it clarifies the inclusion of counteractive measures, cultivating the wisdom that turns toward and destroys afflictions.

True wisdom that is free from delusion is called "non-conceptualization" (amanyanā); true wisdom that realizes the truth is called "wisdom of the true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇajñāna). One should constantly seek this within worldly dharmas.

The phrase "having few desires and being content, yet not abandoning the world" corresponds to the latter part of the preceding verse; it clarifies the inclusion of the *abhidharma* (counteractive dharmas) and the practice of the "vigor of crushing the former māras."
"Having few desires and being content" means personally remaining free from defilement.
"Without abandoning the world" means following along with things that are beneficial.
By diligently practicing this conduct, one thus subdues the works of Māra.
The above section was the first, which, based on the previous resolve for courage, clarified the practice of cultivating remedies to destroy the cycle of birth and death.
From here on, based on the previous aspiration that is free from weariness, it clarifies the cultivation of practices for gathering wholesome qualities.
Within this, the first part clarifies transforming others through the three karmas; the section beginning with "purifying the ten wholesome paths" clarifies possessing one's own virtues.
Within the former, the initial statement, "not violating dignified deportment while being able to conform to worldly customs," clarifies the transformation through bodily karma.

Without violating the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), one is able to conform to worldly customs; worldly laws benefit people, which is to say, without abandoning the Dharma of the Path, one is able to conform to worldly customs.
"Arousing the wisdom of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to guide sentient beings" means that the Dharma of the Path benefits all things.
The section beginning with "Attaining the Compendium of Mindfulness" clarifies the transformation of mental karma (*manas-karman*).
"Attaining the *dhāraṇī* of mindfulness so as not to forget what is heard" clarifies being well-versed in the medicinal teachings of the Dharma.
"Skillfully discerning the various faculties and severing the doubts of sentient beings" indicates knowing the mental capacities of beings.
“Expounding the Dharma without impediment through eloquence” clarifies the transformation of verbal action (*vākkarman*).
What precedes has clarified benefiting others; what follows clarifies one’s own virtues.

Within this, the first section [“admonishing and requesting [the Buddha] to teach”] gathers the wholesome dharmas of ordinary beings; the section following “admonishing and requesting” clarifies gathering the wholesome dharmas of Buddhas; and the section following “deeply cultivating the wholesome” gathers the wholesome dharmas of Bodhisattvas.
Within the summary of all wholesome states, "the pure ten paths of wholesome action" clarifies the cause for cultivating precepts;
"receiving the blessings of humans and devas" clarifies the fruit of possessing precepts.
Receiving the eight superior rewards within the realms of humans and devas is termed "the blessings of humans and devas"; this is the goodness of the desire realm.
"Cultivating the four immeasurables" clarifies the cause for cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Opening the path to the Brahma-heavens" clarifies the result encompassed by that concentration.
Since the four immeasurable minds can produce the fruit of the Brahma-heavens, it is called "opening the path to the Brahma-heavens"; this refers to the wholesome states of the higher realms.
Next is the summary of the Buddha’s virtues:
“Rejoicing in and praising what is good, one obtains the voice of a Buddha,” which signifies the perfection of the Buddha’s vocal karma.
The characteristic of the sound of the Dharma-conch is the voice of a Buddha; it is precisely because one exhorts all Buddhas to preach the Dharma that one obtains the Buddha’s voice.
Furthermore, because one rejoices in and praises the wholesome deeds performed by sentient beings, one attains the voice of a Buddha.
"Wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind results in the majestic deportment of a Buddha" means that one is fully endowed with the bodily karma of a Buddha.
The following clarifies the inclusion and cultivation of the bodhisattva’s wholesome dharmas.
“Cultivating wholesome dharmas deeply so that what arises becomes increasingly superior” refers to the virtues accomplished through cultivation.
There is also a sutra that speaks of “deeply practicing wholesome dharmas,” the meaning of which is similar.
"Establishing the Bodhisattva Saṃgha through the Mahāyāna teachings" means accomplishing virtue by relying on the Dharma.
Because one initiates practice based on the Mahāyāna Dharma, one does not deviate from the virtues of the bodhisattva path; therefore, one succeeds in becoming a member of the Bodhisattva Saṃgha.
"By being heedful in mind, one does not lose any wholesome qualities"—this indicates that virtues are accomplished based on the mind.
Among these three phrases, if we consider the first phrase in terms of its basis, it clarifies excellence; the third [phrase] clarifies the excellence of the mind itself.
Regarding the retribution of the first phrase as that which is accomplished, the second [phrase] excels in person, while the third excels in virtue.
Having extensively analyzed these above, the section beginning with "practicing in this manner" serves as the general conclusion.

Next, the text clarifies that the Bodhisattva does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is presented first by way of question, secondly by way of explanation, and finally by way of summary.
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva not abiding in the unconditioned? is the initial question.
The following provides a detailed analysis.

Within this, the first section clarifies what is cultivated prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), while the section beginning with "contemplating impermanence" clarifies what is accomplished from the stages onward.
Regarding the cultivation prior to the stages, it is practiced according to four gateways: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and non-arising (*anutpāda*).

The essence of all phenomena is empty, which is designated as "emptiness"; within this emptiness, there is no characteristic that can be named, which is designated as "signlessness"; there is no fruit to be produced, which is designated as "wishlessness"; and there is no cause from which they arise, which is called "non-arising."

Although one continues to practice contemplation within these four stages, because one does not dwell in or cling to them, it is said that they are "not realized. Because they are not realized, one is able to give rise to active cultivation (*saṃskāra*).
What has been explained above clarifies the practices cultivated in the mundane realm; what follows below clarifies the supramundane.
In accordance with reality, one correctly contemplates that although the principles are actually simultaneous, they are provisionally distinguished for the sake of exposition.

Among these, the section from the beginning up to "contemplating quiescence" constitutes the understanding of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) within the first stage (*bhūmi*); seeing the four dharmas, such as impermanence and so forth, is precisely what is termed the path of vision.

Regarding the phrase "observing impermanence yet not wearying of the roots of goodness": although one perceives that conditioned phenomena are impermanent and fraught with many faults, one constantly plants roots of goodness therein.
"Observing the suffering of the world yet not loathing birth and death" means that although one knows the faults of suffering, one vows to remain therein constantly to deliver sentient beings.
"Observing non-self yet teaching others without weariness" means that seeing that birth has no reality, one constantly instructs and exhorts others according to provisional names.

"Contemplating quiescent extinction yet not undergoing ultimate extinction" means that although one knows the bliss of the quiescence of nirvana, for the sake of others one remains within existence and does not realize [nirvana] for oneself.
"Contemplating detachment while cultivating goodness of body and mind" refers to the practice of the path on the second stage and above.

Contemplating the ultimate truth (paramārtha) as being free from the characteristics of body and mind is called "contemplating detachment," yet one relies upon body and mind to cultivate the wholesome conduct of wisdom.

On the second stage, upholding the precepts is called "cultivating goodness through the body"; on the third stage, cultivating meditative concentration is called "cultivating goodness through the mind.
"Observing that there is nowhere to which one returns, yet returning to wholesome dharmas" refers to the practice of the compliant patience (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*) on the fourth stage and above.

"Contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as having no point of departure or destination, one cultivates the patient acceptance that accords with reality (*anulomikī kṣānti*); this is the taking of refuge in the land of non-arising wholesome dharmas.
'Contemplating non-arising while bearing all things by means of arising dharmas'—this is the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) on the stages above the seventh."
Although one contemplates that principles are without birth or arising, one constantly manifests birth to teach and transform sentient beings.
"Contemplating the outflow-free while not severing the outflows" refers to the superior practices initiated on the stages above the seventh.

To know that all afflictions are originally quiescent is called contemplating the untainted (*anāsrava*); yet, to constantly manifest the activities of afflictions and karma is called not severing the outflows (*āsrava*).
"Contemplating non-action while employing the practice of dharmas to transform sentient beings" refers to the practice of responding to and transforming sentient beings within the ninth stage.
To realize that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty, quiescent, and non-existent, yet to teach and transform sentient beings through those very phenomena—
this is the mind of transforming sentient beings within the ninth stage, characterized by "contemplating emptiness and non-existence while not abandoning great compassion."
Although he knows that sentient beings are empty and non-existent, he cherishes them with great equanimity and great compassion.

Furthermore, the preceding phrase clarifies his compassionate benefit by means of active teaching and transformation, while this [present] passage demonstrates his compassionate benefit by not abandoning them through compassion.
"Observing the stage of the True Dharma (saddharmapada) without following the Lesser Vehicle" refers to the firmness of the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) within the ten stages.
Observing that the essence of phenomena is empty is called the stage of the True Dharma; because one does not cling to emptiness, one does not fall into the Lesser Vehicle.
"Contemplating phenomena as illusory" means knowing that phenomena exist only as provisional designations.
"Lacking solidity," and so forth, means knowing that phenomena are truly non-existent.
Within illusory phenomena there is no real or solid nature; therefore, they are said to lack solidity.
The emptiness of the self and the person is called "no person as master.
The conventional designations of "sentient being" and "characteristics" are both non-existent; this is called "signlessness.
The following clarifies non-attachment.
As they engage in practice according to their circumstances, they recall the vows they originally made in the past seeking to become Buddhas.
Because the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) have not yet been fulfilled, this is called "the original mind being unfulfilled."
One undertakes the practices of cultivation in order to fulfill those vows; therefore, these are called "non-wasteful merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
They are termed "non-wasteful" because they are practiced with a sincere mind. The practices of giving, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence are designated as "merit."
Dhyāna is called the pāramitā of meditation; wisdom is precisely the prajñā-pāramitā.
These are provisionally distinguished according to their characteristics and stages, yet they cannot be definitively fixed.
This has been extensively analyzed above.
The phrase "cultivating in this way" below serves as a general conclusion.
In the preceding section, which begins with the initial practice, the meaning of neither abiding nor exhausting was clarified;
next, in the subsequent section concerning the final accomplishment of practice, the meaning of non-exhaustion is clarified.
Among these four pairs, the first pair concerns self-benefit and the latter three concern benefiting others.

Within the former [category of] self-benefit, regarding the phrase "furthermore, possessing merit, one does not abide in non-existence": because merit follows along with existence, one does not abide in non-existence.

Regarding the phrase "Because they possess wisdom, they do not exhaust existence": through wisdom, one knows that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are illusory transformations and lack reality; thus, one does not fear them, but is always able to abide within them. Therefore, by possessing wisdom, one does not exhaust conditioned existence.

Regarding the subsequent section on benefiting others: the first pair marks the beginning of benefiting others, the second pair represents the middle stage of benefiting others, and the third pair constitutes the conclusion of benefiting others.
Regarding the first pair of opposites: "Because of great compassion, one does not abide in non-existence" means that because compassion follows after existence, one does not abide in non-existence.

"Because of fulfilling original vows, one does not exhaust existence" means that since original vows consist of constantly transforming sentient beings within existence, one does not exhaust existence in order to fulfill them now.

In the second pair, regarding the phrase "because of gathering the medicine of the Dharma, one does not abide in non-existence": seeking from a teacher the methods for transforming sentient beings is called "gathering the medicine of the Dharma.
Because this seeking for the Dharma exists within the realm of existence, one does not abide in non-existence.
Regarding the phrase "it is not exhausted because it accords with the medicine," this means that because he universally bestows the Dharma upon sentient beings without ceasing, it is not exhausted.

In the third pair, regarding "knowing the illnesses of sentient beings and not abiding in non-existence," this means that because he knows illness exists within existence, he does not abide in non-existence.

Regarding the phrase "the extinction of the illnesses of sentient beings is not yet exhaustive": because the arising of illnesses is boundless and their extinction is difficult to exhaust, they are said to be not yet exhausted.
First, there was a general exhortation to study; next, there was a specific instruction; finally, this is the concluding summary of the exhortation.
The phrase "all you noble beings" is an address to those being exhorted.

"That Bodhisattvas have already cultivated the non-exhaustion of the conditioned and the non-abiding in the unconditioned is called the Dharma-gate of the liberation of exhaustion and non-exhaustion" is the concluding statement.
"Thus you should train yourselves" is an exhortation to study.

The preceding section describes how the various bodhisattvas returned to their lands after the Buddha had taught them the dharmas; the following section clarifies that the bodhisattvas, having heard the Dharma with joy, paid homage, offered praise, and departed.
Within this, first there is the reverent service through the three types of action, followed by the departure to return to their own lands.
Regarding the former, the initial statement, "Those bodhisattvas rejoiced upon hearing the teaching," refers to the joy of mental action (*manas-karman*).
The passage beginning with "With various flowers" and so forth refers to physical offerings.
Within this, one first makes offerings to the Triple Gem through material things such as incense and flowers, and subsequently performs prostrations.

Among the offerings, "scattering various wonderful flowers of diverse colors and diverse fragrances throughout the three thousandfold world system to make offerings to the Buddha" constitutes the offering to the Buddha-jewel.
"Furthermore, this sutra and its Dharma" refers to making offerings to the Jewel of the Dharma.
"Together with all the bodhisattvas" refers to making offerings to the Jewel of the Sangha.
Thus far has been the section on making offerings.
"Performing rites for them below" completes the discussion of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
"Praising their virtues" and so forth refers to verbal praise (*vākkarman*).
The above constitutes respectful service and sustenance.
"The statement 'having spoken, he disappeared and returned to his own country' means that he took his leave and returned to his native land.
— *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 4, Part 1.
